title: FESS quick mocks
description: All 196 supplied revision points in short practice sets, with explanations and current-source revision notes.

questions.question: What is a realistic commercial risk if a company loses a required third-party approval or certification?

options.text: It may lose access to contracts or tenders that require that approval.
options.explanation: Customers and specifications may require a particular approval.

options.text: It automatically loses every existing contract.
options.explanation: The effect depends on contractual requirements; it is not automatically universal.

options.text: Its electrical test instruments stop working.
options.explanation: Certification status does not physically disable equipment.

options.text: It is guaranteed to win more tenders.
options.explanation: Losing a required approval does not create that guarantee.

questions.explanation: Approval schemes can affect customer confidence and eligibility for work. Identify the actual contractual and scheme requirements rather than assuming the same consequence in every case.

questions.question: Why does consistently good customer service matter to a fire and security business?

options.text: It removes the need for competent technical work.
options.explanation: Good manners do not replace technical competence.

options.text: It helps build trust, clear communication and lasting customer relationships.
options.explanation: Reliable communication and service support confidence and retention.

options.text: It guarantees that every customer will renew forever.
options.explanation: Good service helps relationships but cannot guarantee future decisions.

options.text: It allows agreed requirements to be ignored.
options.explanation: Customer service includes understanding and meeting appropriate requirements.

questions.explanation: Technical quality and clear, respectful service work together. Highfield’s customer-service criteria include professional image, stakeholder relationships and commercial risk.

questions.question: Which response best starts an effective complaint-handling process?

options.text: Promise an immediate fix before checking what happened.
options.explanation: An unsupported promise can make the complaint worse.

options.text: Give no contact details until the customer complains again.
options.explanation: That obstructs useful communication and follow-up.

options.text: Acknowledge the issue, identify the contact, explain the next action and give a realistic response time.
options.explanation: The customer needs a clear and accountable next step.

options.text: Argue about blame before listening to the complaint.
options.explanation: That can prevent the actual concern being understood.

questions.explanation: Use the organisation’s complaint process and record the agreed next steps. Explain who will respond, how and when; update the customer if the timetable changes.

questions.question: What is a useful benefit of applying an internal quality standard consistently?

options.text: All faults become impossible.
options.explanation: A process can improve quality but cannot guarantee no faults.

options.text: Inspection and records are no longer needed.
options.explanation: Checks and records usually form part of the quality process.

options.text: Each engineer can ignore the agreed specification.
options.explanation: Consistency requires the applicable specification to be followed.

options.text: Different engineers work to defined, repeatable requirements and checks.
options.explanation: A common process reduces avoidable variation.

questions.explanation: Internal standards help make work consistent and reviewable. They support, rather than replace, competent workmanship, manufacturer requirements and appropriate testing.

questions.question: What should an internal company code of practice provide?

options.text: A consistent, documented way to meet the company’s work and quality requirements.
options.explanation: Engineers need an agreed process rather than individual guesswork.

options.text: Permission to override the law.
options.explanation: A company procedure cannot remove legal duties.

options.text: A substitute for every manufacturer’s instructions.
options.explanation: Equipment-specific requirements still apply.

options.text: A different unrecorded rule for every engineer.
options.explanation: Uncontrolled variation defeats a common code of practice.

questions.explanation: A company code can organise working methods and quality checks. It must fit applicable law, standards, contracts and product instructions; it is not the same thing as an HSE Approved Code of Practice.

questions.question: Which pair are examples of cloud file-sharing services that can provide a link to send by email?

options.text: A multimeter and a clamp meter.
options.explanation: These are test instruments, not cloud file-sharing services.

options.text: Dropbox and SharePoint.
options.explanation: Both provide file-sharing links and access controls.

options.text: A resistor and a rectifier.
options.explanation: These are electronic components.

options.text: A zone chart and a bell box.
options.explanation: These are not cloud file-sharing services.

questions.explanation: A sharing link can avoid a large email attachment, but permissions still matter. Check the intended recipients and access level; do not make sensitive customer documents public by default.

questions.question: You need to send a private service update to one customer. How should the channel be chosen?

options.text: Post it publicly because social media reaches groups.
options.explanation: A private update may expose sensitive information if posted publicly.

options.text: Always use the same channel regardless of accessibility needs.
options.explanation: The method should suit the audience and context.

options.text: Use an authorised channel appropriate to that customer and the sensitivity of the information.
options.explanation: The audience, consent and confidentiality determine the suitable channel.

options.text: Send it to every customer to save time.
options.explanation: Other customers are not automatically authorised recipients.

questions.explanation: Email may suit an individual update; a group announcement needs its own agreed audience and permissions. “Email for one, social media for many” is not a universal rule.
questions.revisionNote: The uploaded guide’s channel examples are simplified. Choose by purpose, privacy and customer needs.

questions.question: Which software function is intended to detect and remove or quarantine malware on a laptop?

options.text: A screen-brightness control.
options.explanation: It changes the display, not malware protection.

options.text: A PDF page-number setting.
options.explanation: It does not inspect the computer for threats.

options.text: A wallpaper theme.
options.explanation: Changing appearance does not remove malware.

options.text: Updated antivirus or endpoint-protection software.
options.explanation: Its threat-protection features scan and respond to malware.

questions.explanation: Keep protection and the operating system updated and follow the organisation’s incident process. Antivirus helps manage threats; it does not guarantee that every attack is blocked.

questions.question: During a customer explanation, which behaviour is most likely to appear disengaged if done deliberately without explanation?

options.text: Turning away and repeatedly checking unrelated messages while they speak.
options.explanation: This interrupts attention to the person and their concern.

options.text: Checking your understanding with a relevant question.
options.explanation: That usually demonstrates active engagement.

options.text: Offering a written summary when requested.
options.explanation: That adapts communication to the person’s needs.

options.text: Allowing the customer time to finish their explanation.
options.explanation: Listening without interruption can support clear communication.

questions.explanation: Pay attention and adapt communication respectfully. Do not assume that a particular posture, eye-contact pattern or facial expression proves someone’s attitude or ability.
questions.revisionNote: The original body-language examples are not universal rules; context, culture and disability can affect non-verbal communication.

questions.question: A customer complains that the visit took longer than expected. What is the best response?

options.text: Dismiss the concern because the technical work is finished.
options.explanation: The customer’s experience and agreed arrangements still matter.

options.text: Listen, explain the relevant causes calmly and agree the next steps.
options.explanation: This addresses the concern while keeping the discussion constructive.

options.text: Invent a reason that sounds more convincing.
options.explanation: Misleading information damages trust and records.

options.text: Blame the customer before reviewing the facts.
options.explanation: That can escalate the dispute and miss the actual issue.

questions.explanation: Use factual, understandable language and the complaint process if needed. Explain what happened, what was done and any follow-up without making unsupported promises.

questions.question: A customer says they have hearing loss. What should you do first when agreeing how to explain the system?

options.text: Assume they can lip-read.
options.explanation: Not everyone lip-reads or finds it sufficient.

options.text: Rule out an interpreter without asking about their needs.
options.explanation: Appropriate communication support may be needed.

options.text: Ask which communication method works best for them and adapt accordingly.
options.explanation: The person can tell you what support or format is useful.

options.text: Only speak to another person and ignore the customer.
options.explanation: Do not exclude the customer from their own information.

questions.explanation: Use the person’s preferred reasonable communication method and check understanding. Clear speech, written information, visual support or an interpreter may be appropriate depending on the person.
questions.revisionNote: The guide’s claim that a person can probably lip-read, and its blanket advice against an interpreter, should not be treated as correct.

questions.question: For an agreed routine appointment update to an existing customer, what makes an email appropriate?

options.text: It is always informal, whatever the subject.
options.explanation: Tone and formality depend on context, including complaints or contractual matters.

options.text: It contains unexplained technical abbreviations.
options.explanation: The reader must be able to understand the message.

options.text: It includes other customers’ private details.
options.explanation: Those details are unrelated and may be confidential.

options.text: It is clear, professional, addressed correctly and suitable for the information being sent.
options.explanation: The message should suit the purpose and intended recipient.

questions.explanation: Use a suitable tone, useful subject and clear actions or dates. Follow the organisation’s correspondence and complaint procedures; an existing relationship does not make every message informal.

questions.question: In the organisation name NSI, what does the I stand for?

options.text: Inspectorate.
options.explanation: NSI is the National Security Inspectorate.

options.text: Installation.
options.explanation: That is not the word used in the organisation’s name.

options.text: Insurance.
options.explanation: NSI is not an abbreviation for National Security Insurance.

options.text: Institute.
options.explanation: The official name uses Inspectorate.

questions.explanation: The full name is National Security Inspectorate. Keep an organisation’s identity separate from the particular approval scheme or inspection requirements relevant to a business.

questions.question: Which statement about repeatedly arriving late to agreed visits is most defensible?

options.text: It cannot affect a company’s costs or budget.
options.explanation: Lost time and disrupted work can have financial consequences.

options.text: It can affect customer trust, scheduling and business costs.
options.explanation: The effects can include reputation, disruption and wasted resources.

options.text: It always improves the professional image.
options.explanation: Repeated unexplained lateness is unlikely to build confidence.

options.text: Only the engineer can be affected.
options.explanation: Customers and other workers may also be affected.

questions.explanation: Plan realistically and communicate unavoidable delays promptly. The actual consequences depend on the job, but it is unsafe to memorise “lateness never affects the budget.”
questions.revisionNote: The original suggested that annual budgets are unaffected. That is not a reliable general rule.

questions.question: Which subject is principally covered by the Workplace (Health, Safety and Welfare) Regulations 1992?

options.text: Only the programming of fire alarm panels.
options.explanation: The regulations have a much wider workplace scope.

options.text: Only customer data retention periods.
options.explanation: That is not their principal subject.

options.text: Basic workplace conditions such as ventilation, lighting, cleanliness and welfare facilities.
options.explanation: These are central health, safety and welfare conditions covered by the regulations.

options.text: Only which alarm brand may be installed.
options.explanation: They do not select equipment brands.

questions.explanation: HSE describes a wide range of basic workplace health, safety and welfare issues. Applicability and exceptions must be checked for the actual workplace.

questions.question: Which regulations specifically address suitable work equipment, its maintenance and adequate training for its use?

options.text: The UK GDPR alone.
options.explanation: Data protection law does not replace work-equipment duties.

options.text: A supplier’s advertising policy.
options.explanation: Advertising is not the relevant work-equipment regulation.

options.text: The customer’s colour-scheme specification.
options.explanation: Appearance requirements do not govern equipment safety training.

options.text: PUWER: Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998.
options.explanation: PUWER concerns work equipment and the people using or managing it.

questions.explanation: PUWER includes suitability, maintenance, inspection where necessary, information and training. Wider risk-management duties also apply; the question is specifically about work equipment.
questions.revisionNote: The original prompt could refer to more than one regulation. This wording establishes the work-equipment context.

questions.question: Under HSE’s summary of the Noise at Work Regulations, which daily or weekly average exposure level triggers provision of hearing protection and hearing-protection zones?

options.explanation: HSE gives 85 dB(A) as the upper exposure action level for these measures.

options.text: 85 volts.
options.explanation: Volts measure electrical potential, not noise exposure.

options.text: Any single sound reading of 85 dB, with no duration context.
options.explanation: The stated action value concerns daily or weekly exposure, not just one unspecified reading.

options.text: Only 120 dB(A) averaged over the week.
options.explanation: That is not the action value HSE specifies.

questions.explanation: Use exposure assessment and the required controls, not a bare noise number. Visual fire-warning provision needs its own fire-risk and system-design assessment.
questions.revisionNote: The guide omits exposure duration and incorrectly turns this threshold into a blanket rule that VADs must always be fitted above it.

questions.question: Which HSE guidance note addresses electrical test equipment for use on low-voltage electrical systems?

options.text: A site’s Wi-Fi password policy.
options.explanation: That is unrelated to safe electrical test equipment.

options.text: GS38.
options.explanation: GS38 is HSE guidance for electrical test equipment used on low-voltage systems.

options.text: A CCTV recording schedule.
options.explanation: It does not specify electrical test-equipment precautions.

options.text: A detector’s paint-colour reference.
options.explanation: That does not establish suitable test equipment.

questions.explanation: Select suitable test equipment and follow the applicable safe isolation procedure, including proving the detector before and after use where required. GS38 is guidance, not a claim that any device marked “tester” is suitable.

questions.question: What does RAMS normally refer to in site-work planning?

options.text: Remote Alarm Memory Storage.
options.explanation: That is not the site-planning meaning of RAMS.

options.text: Resistor Accuracy Measurement System.
options.explanation: That is not the intended term.

options.text: Risk Assessment and Method Statement.
options.explanation: It combines assessment of the risks with the planned safe method of work.

options.text: Routine Access Menu Selection.
options.explanation: That describes neither risk assessment nor a method statement.

questions.explanation: The risk assessment identifies and controls hazards; the method statement explains how the work will be carried out safely. Keep the documents suitable for the actual task and changing conditions.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a permit-to-work system for a specified hazardous task?

options.text: Permission to ignore the risk assessment.
options.explanation: The permit depends on appropriate risk assessment and precautions.

options.text: A guarantee that no hazard can exist.
options.explanation: A permit is a control process, not a guarantee.

options.text: Unlimited authorisation for any work at any later date.
options.explanation: The scope and time of the permitted work are controlled.

options.text: Formal authorisation defining the work, precautions, responsibilities and controlled period.
options.explanation: The permit coordinates the task and its required safety arrangements.

questions.explanation: A permit must be understood, observed and properly closed or handed back. It does not make an unsafe task safe merely by being signed.

questions.question: For corded tools on a construction site, which reduced low-voltage AC system is commonly used to reduce shock risk?

options.text: A suitable 110 V centre-tapped-to-earth supply.
options.explanation: This is the reduced low-voltage arrangement described by HSE for site tools.

options.text: A 230 V extension lead with the earth removed.
options.explanation: Removing protective earthing is dangerous and not the intended arrangement.

options.text: Any yellow cable, regardless of its actual supply.
options.explanation: Colour alone does not establish voltage or protection.

options.text: An unapproved homemade transformer connection.
options.explanation: The system must be suitable and properly designed, not improvised.

questions.explanation: HSE also recommends battery-operated equipment where suitable. The centre-tapped arrangement limits each live conductor’s voltage to earth; it is not permission to work on live equipment.
questions.revisionNote: The guide’s “preferred voltage” shorthand is expanded: cordless equipment can remove leads, and 110 V must be a suitable reduced-low-voltage arrangement.

questions.question: You are asked to use unfamiliar access equipment for which you lack the necessary training. What should you do?

options.text: Try it first and ask for help only if it goes wrong.
options.explanation: Experimenting with unfamiliar work equipment can create serious risk.

options.text: Do not operate it unsupervised; tell the responsible manager and arrange appropriate training or competent assistance.
options.explanation: The task must be allocated to someone with the required competence and arrangements.

options.text: Assume another type of equipment is close enough.
options.explanation: Different equipment can have different hazards and controls.

options.text: Rely on being told it is easy.
options.explanation: Reassurance is not evidence of competence or training.

questions.explanation: Explain the limitation and follow the site’s training and authorisation arrangements. Competence must match the equipment and task.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes HSE from an ACOP?

options.text: ACOP means a private company’s “accepted code of practice”.
options.explanation: That is not the official meaning of ACOP.

options.text: An ACOP automatically replaces the law.
options.explanation: It describes ways of complying with duties; the law remains applicable.

options.text: HSE is the regulator; an ACOP is an Approved Code of Practice with a special legal status.
options.explanation: HSE explains the legal status of its published Approved Codes of Practice.

options.text: HSE is simply another name for a company handbook.
options.explanation: HSE is the Health and Safety Executive.

questions.explanation: An ACOP is not itself the same as a regulation, but has a special legal status in proceedings. An alternative method may comply with the law if it meets the relevant duty.
questions.revisionNote: The uploaded answer misdefines ACOP and wrongly treats it as an individual company’s rules.

questions.question: Which would be unacceptable at system handover?

options.text: Applicable certificates and commissioning records.
options.explanation: These can be required handover evidence.

options.text: As-fitted information and system-specific operating instructions.
options.explanation: These help the responsible person operate and maintain the actual installation.

options.text: A record of agreed variations and relevant outstanding matters.
options.explanation: These prevent deviations or incomplete work being hidden.

options.text: An unrecorded verbal claim that all documentation can be skipped.
options.explanation: Verbal reassurance cannot replace the required records and instructions.

questions.explanation: The required package depends on the system and specification. Provide appropriate certificates, records, drawings, instructions and user information rather than relying on a generic list alone.

questions.question: Which standards family covers video-surveillance systems for security applications in current FESS references?

options.text: BS EN 62676.
options.explanation: Highfield’s current K1 explicitly identifies BS EN 62676 for video surveillance.

options.text: BS EN 50131 only.
options.explanation: That family concerns intrusion and hold-up alarm systems.

options.text: BS 5839 only.
options.explanation: That is the fire-detection and fire-alarm family.

options.text: BS EN 60839-11 only.
options.explanation: That is the electronic access-control part of the alarm/security family.

questions.explanation: Select the relevant part and current applicable edition for the task. BS EN 50132-7 is a legacy reference; do not treat an old guide’s number as the current application document.
questions.revisionNote: The guide already notes a replacement; this question teaches the current family rather than asserting an unchecked edition of every part.

questions.question: Which standards family specifically covers electronic access-control system and component requirements and application guidance?

options.text: BS EN 62676 only.
options.explanation: That family concerns video-surveillance systems.
Part 11-1 covers system/components and Part 11-2 covers application guidance.

options.text: BS 5839 only.
options.explanation: That family concerns fire detection and fire alarms.

options.text: An IP ingress-protection code alone.
options.explanation: Ingress protection does not specify the complete access-control system requirements.

questions.explanation: Use the applicable part and edition. Powered-door safety requirements can also apply, but a door-safety standard is not a substitute for electronic access-control requirements.
questions.revisionNote: BS EN 50133-1 in the uploaded guide is a legacy reference. Electronic access control is addressed by BS EN 60839-11.

questions.question: Which description best matches Category L3 in Hochiki’s BS 5839-1:2025 overview?

options.text: A manual-only system with no automatic detection.
options.explanation: That describes Category M, not L3.

options.text: An arbitrary arrangement with no stated fire-risk objective.
options.explanation: L5 is risk-objective based; it is not simply anywhere someone wants detection.

options.text: Automatic detection on escape routes and in rooms opening onto those routes.
options.explanation: This extends the L4 escape-route approach to rooms opening onto the routes.

options.text: Only property protection in selected areas.
options.explanation: That describes the broad purpose of P2, not an L life-protection category.

questions.explanation: L categories concern life protection: L4 escape routes; L3 adds rooms opening onto them; L2 adds defined risk areas; L1 has broad coverage with permitted exceptions; L5 serves a specified risk objective. The detailed design requires the applicable standard.
questions.revisionNote: Use categories rather than “grades”. The uploaded “L1 in ALL rooms” and “L5 anywhere they want” omit important qualifications.

questions.question: For a wall-mounted VAD, what minimum height above finished floor level is stated in Hochiki’s BS 5839-1:2025 pocket guide?

options.text: Any height is acceptable if the light is bright.
options.explanation: Brightness alone does not establish coverage or installation suitability.

options.text: The number in a W rating is always a universal minimum height.
options.explanation: A W rating describes the rated coverage volume and mounting condition, not a blanket minimum.

options.text: Always 9 m, regardless of device rating.
options.explanation: That is not the wall-mounting minimum stated by the guide.

options.text: 2.1 m, while also meeting the device’s coverage and installation requirements.
options.explanation: The cited guide states this wall-mounting minimum.

questions.explanation: Distinguish the installation minimum from the rated coverage volume and maximum mounting condition. Apply the actual manufacturer’s instructions and the system design; ceiling-mounted categories are different.
questions.revisionNote: The guide’s 2.1 m wall-mounting point is retained, but qualified to avoid confusing it with a W-category coverage rating.

questions.question: What general MCP mounting height and tolerance does Hochiki’s BS 5839-1:2025 overview state?

options.text: 1.4 m above finished floor, with +200 mm / −300 mm tolerance.
options.explanation: That is the asymmetric tolerance stated in the current overview.

options.text: 1.4 m with ±300 mm in both directions.
options.explanation: The cited upper tolerance is +200 mm, not +300 mm.

options.text: Every call point must be exactly 1.2 m with no variation.
options.explanation: That is not the general rule stated by the source; specific accessibility requirements still need consideration.

options.text: Anywhere below the ceiling.
options.explanation: That does not satisfy the stated mounting guidance.

questions.explanation: Check the actual design, accessibility needs and any agreed variations. The cited guide says positioning below 1.1 m requires a variation; do not treat this short question as the complete design specification.
questions.revisionNote: The uploaded ±300 mm wording is corrected to +200/−300 mm. Accessibility and approved variations must be considered in the actual design.

questions.question: What should guide selection of steel cable tray for an exposed outdoor location?

options.text: Indoor suitability alone.
options.explanation: An indoor finish may not suit outdoor exposure.

options.text: A corrosion-protection system suitable for the environment, with cut edges and damage treated as specified.
options.explanation: The finish and its installation details affect corrosion resistance.

options.text: Removing the protective coating to make it look uniform.
options.explanation: That can reduce corrosion protection.

options.text: Assuming any painted tray is suitable for every coastal environment.
options.explanation: The actual environment and product specification matter.

questions.explanation: Select containment and protective finishes for the actual environment. Exposed steel requires suitable corrosion protection; a galvanised finish is not a guarantee of suitability in every corrosive environment. Follow the specified product instructions and installation design.
questions.revisionNote: The original “galvanised” answer is expanded: exposure severity and manufacturer-specified finish/repair details still matter.

questions.question: How should the required mains protective-device or fused-spur rating for a particular panel be selected?

options.text: Always fit 3 A regardless of the panel.
options.explanation: A commonly encountered value is not a universal manufacturer requirement.

options.text: Choose the largest fuse that physically fits.
options.explanation: Physical fit does not establish safe protection.

options.text: From the applicable panel instructions and circuit design, not a universal “all panels” value.
options.explanation: Ratings and protective arrangements depend on the equipment and circuit.

options.text: Copy the panel’s internal fuse rating without checking the supply requirements.
options.explanation: Internal and upstream protection serve different design requirements.

questions.explanation: Identify the exact model, supply arrangement and applicable design. Do not confuse an internal board fuse, PSU rating and upstream circuit protection.
questions.revisionNote: The uploaded “most panels = 3 A” is not taught as a universal rule. The manufacturer’s stated rating must be checked.

questions.question: What is the role of a suitably designed catenary support wire in an authorised overhead cable installation?

options.text: It automatically provides the cable’s data protocol.
options.explanation: Mechanical support does not determine communication protocol.

options.text: It removes the need to assess clearances and structural loads.
options.explanation: The entire installation still needs suitable design and approval.

options.text: It makes any indoor cable suitable for outdoor exposure.
options.explanation: The cable’s environmental rating remains separate.

options.text: It provides mechanical support so the cable is not relied on to carry the unsupported span’s tension.
options.explanation: The support system carries the intended mechanical load.

questions.explanation: A catenary is a mechanical support method, not permission to improvise an overhead crossing. Check cable suitability, span loads, fixings, clearances and the installation specification.
questions.revisionNote: The supporting-wire concept is retained with design qualifications; it is not a generic instruction to span buildings.

questions.question: What does an RCD respond to in its protective function?

options.text: Residual current: an imbalance in the current flowing in the circuit’s live conductors.
options.explanation: Current returning by an unintended path can create a residual-current imbalance.

options.text: Only the colour of the cable insulation.
options.explanation: Colour does not trigger the device.

options.text: Every possible electric shock with guaranteed protection.
options.explanation: An RCD cannot protect against every type of shock.

options.text: Only a low standby-battery voltage.
options.explanation: That is not its residual-current protective function.

questions.explanation: An RCD is an additional protective measure, not a substitute for secure isolation. Devices have specified types, ratings and test requirements; 30 mA is not the rating of every RCD.
questions.revisionNote: The original wording confuses the current path and treats approximately 30 mA as universal. The residual-current principle and rating qualification are clearer.

questions.question: Within its specified operating limits, what is the basic rectifying action of a conventional diode?

options.text: It is an ideal conductor in both directions.
options.explanation: That is not rectifying behaviour.

options.text: It conducts much more readily in the forward direction than in reverse.
options.explanation: Forward and reverse bias produce very different conduction behaviour.

options.text: It stores a permanent software address.
options.explanation: A diode does not perform that configuration function.

options.text: It always blocks every current in both directions.
options.explanation: A forward-biased diode is intended to conduct under suitable conditions.

questions.explanation: Real diodes have forward voltage, leakage, current and reverse-voltage limits. “One-way” is a useful introduction, not a claim of ideal behaviour under every voltage.

questions.question: Why must a cable meet its specified conductor material, size and resistance requirements?

options.text: Higher resistance always gives the load more voltage.
options.explanation: Higher resistance causes a greater drop at the same current.

options.text: A matching outer colour proves the conductor specification.
options.explanation: Appearance does not prove the conductor material or resistance.

options.text: Excessive conductor resistance can increase voltage drop and affect performance.
options.explanation: For the stated current, Vdrop = I × R.

options.text: The conductor has no effect once the cable is long enough.
options.explanation: Cable length and conductor properties affect resistance.

questions.explanation: Specify and verify the actual cable, not just a claim about “copper content”. Material, cross-section, length, joints and operating conditions all influence the circuit.
questions.revisionNote: The uploaded copper-content explanation is reframed around verified conductor specification and resistance, rather than an undefined purity rule.

questions.question: Which pair of functions can transistors perform in appropriately designed electronic circuits?

options.text: Only mechanical cable support.
options.explanation: That is not a transistor function.

options.text: Only storing a fuse’s melting point.
options.explanation: That does not describe transistor operation.

options.text: Automatically converting every input to exactly 0.7 V.
options.explanation: There is no universal fixed output voltage of that kind.

options.text: Signal amplification and electronic switching.
options.explanation: Transistors can be used in amplifier or switching circuits.

questions.explanation: Different transistor types and circuits work differently. A silicon BJT’s approximate base-emitter behaviour must not be generalised into “all transistors use 0.7 V to switch a larger voltage.”
questions.revisionNote: The original 0.7 V description is not universal and mixes device behaviour with amplification. The question uses the supported functional principle.

questions.question: Ideal 4 Ω and 1 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?

options.explanation: That would be the series total.
Subtracting values is not the parallel-resistance rule.
The additional parallel path reduces the equivalent resistance.

questions.explanation: For two positive resistors in parallel, the equivalent is less than either branch. Use the formula to obtain the value rather than relying only on a multiple-choice shortcut.

questions.question: Which term describes a network connecting separate local networks over a wider geographical area?

options.text: A single resistor’s tolerance band.
options.explanation: That is unrelated to network scope.

options.text: WAN: wide area network.
options.explanation: A WAN links networks across wider geographical areas.

options.text: Only a Wi-Fi connection inside one room.
options.explanation: That is a local connection, not inherently a WAN.

options.text: A requirement that every device use a different electrical frequency.
options.explanation: That does not define a WAN.

questions.explanation: The internet is a major example of interconnected networks, but WAN does not mean only the public internet. IP can be used on both local and wide-area networks.
questions.revisionNote: The uploaded wording blurs IP, LAN, WAN and the internet. These are related concepts, not interchangeable names.

questions.question: What does a data rate stated as bit/s or bps describe?

options.text: The number of bytes stored permanently.
options.explanation: Storage size and transfer rate are different quantities.

options.text: Battery voltage per second.
options.explanation: That is not the meaning of bps.

options.text: The number of bits transferred per second.
options.explanation: The unit is bits per second.

options.text: Cable resistance in ohms.
options.explanation: Resistance uses a different unit.

questions.explanation: Keep bits and bytes distinct: one byte normally contains eight bits. A stated bit rate alone does not guarantee cable length, usable throughput or compatibility.

questions.question: What makes remote alarm signalling more than a local bell or sounder?

options.text: The communicator has a familiar brand label, even if not commissioned.
options.explanation: A label does not prove that the service works.

options.text: The local sounder is loud enough to be heard everywhere.
options.explanation: A local audible warning is not remote signalling.

options.text: A network cable is plugged in, regardless of ARC receipt.
options.explanation: Physical connection alone does not demonstrate correct delivery or supervision.

options.text: It communicates relevant alarm or status information to the configured receiving service, with the specified path supervision.
options.explanation: Remote signalling involves an actual communication service and its agreed supervision.

questions.explanation: Use the current communicator and service documentation and verify signals with the authorised receiving centre arrangements. Brand examples are not evidence that a particular path or service is commissioned.
questions.revisionNote: Treat Redcare and other names in the older guide as examples from that period, not a current service-availability guarantee.

questions.question: What is the declared nominal frequency of the UK public electricity supply under the cited regulations?

options.text: 50 Hz.
options.explanation: Regulation 27 specifies a declared frequency of 50 hertz.

options.text: 50 volts.
options.explanation: Volts measure potential difference, not frequency.
230 is the nominal phase-to-neutral voltage figure, not the frequency.

options.text: Always 60 Hz throughout the UK.
options.explanation: That is not the frequency stated by the cited UK regulations.

questions.explanation: Hertz means cycles per second. The cited low-voltage phase-to-neutral declared value is 230 V, subject to the permitted variations; do not memorise 220 V as the UK declared nominal value.
questions.revisionNote: The guide’s 50 Hz answer is retained; its accompanying 220 V wording is updated to the declared 230 V nominal supply.

questions.question: What does an enclosure’s IP code principally describe?

options.text: The camera’s internet-protocol address.
options.explanation: An enclosure IP code is a different use of the letters IP.

options.text: Its classified protection against access/solid objects and water ingress.
options.explanation: The code addresses specified ingress-protection tests.

options.text: A guarantee of resistance to every chemical and weather condition.
options.explanation: The code does not establish every environmental property.

options.text: The remaining battery runtime.
options.explanation: Ingress protection does not measure stored energy.

questions.explanation: Check the exact digits, test conditions and product instructions. An IP rating alone does not prove corrosion resistance, UV resistance or suitability for every outdoor location.

questions.question: Before deciding the required standby time for an intruder system, what must be established?

options.text: Only that the system is called “unmonitored”.
options.explanation: That label alone does not establish every design requirement.

options.text: One universal duration for every intruder and fire system.
options.explanation: Different systems and configurations have different requirements.

options.text: The applicable system grade, power-supply arrangement, monitoring requirements and documented design.
options.explanation: The required capacity and duration depend on the actual applicable requirements.

options.text: The battery’s physical size alone.
options.explanation: Size alone does not establish required standby performance.

questions.explanation: Use the applicable standards, power-supply type and manufacturer documentation to calculate and test the actual requirement. Do not transfer a duration from another grade or a fire-system example.
questions.revisionNote: The uploaded fixed-hour examples are not a complete rule. This question deliberately tests the configuration needed before selecting the applicable requirement.

questions.question: What does LSF normally stand for in cable descriptions?

options.text: Low signal frequency only.
options.explanation: That is not the usual cable-material meaning.

options.text: Long steel fixing.
options.explanation: That is not the cable classification.

options.text: A guarantee of zero halogens and fire survival.
options.explanation: Those are separate properties requiring their own specifications.

options.text: Low smoke and fume.
options.explanation: That is the usual expansion of the abbreviation.

questions.explanation: Check the cable’s declared tests and material specification. LSF wording alone does not establish LSZH/LS0H performance or the circuit integrity required of a fire-resisting cable.
questions.revisionNote: Do not equate a low-smoke/fume description with zero halogen content or continued operation during a fire.

questions.question: A lock has a nominal rating of 600 lbf. Using 1 lbf ≈ 4.448 N, what is the approximate rated force in newtons?

options.text: 2,669 N, or about 2.67 kN.

options.explanation: Pounds-force and newtons are not equal units.
That reverses the supplied conversion.
That introduces an extra factor of ten.

questions.explanation: This converts the stated nominal rating; it does not guarantee the installed holding force. Alignment, mounting, surface condition and the exact product specification still matter.
questions.revisionNote: The original range uses rough conversions and typical product sizes. Here the conversion factor and nominal rating are explicit, avoiding a universal maglock range.

questions.question: For a high-risk site, how should the required alarm-transmission performance be selected?

options.text: Always choose the cheapest path without checking requirements.
options.explanation: Cost alone does not establish suitable signalling performance.

options.text: From the risk assessment, specification and applicable alarm-transmission category and service requirements.
options.explanation: The required reporting and resilience must fit the actual design.

options.text: Assume an old grade number fixes every current reporting time.
options.explanation: Categories, configurations and applicable editions need checking.

options.text: Choose only by the communicator’s colour.
options.explanation: Appearance does not establish signalling performance.

questions.explanation: Check the specified path arrangement, reporting requirements and receiving-centre service. Do not substitute a memorised historic “grade number = timeout” table for the current applicable requirements.
questions.revisionNote: The guide’s 25-hour/4-minute shorthand is not presented as a universal current alarm-transmission rule.

questions.question: Why is “RS-485 always works over 1,200 m” an incomplete installation rule?

options.text: RS-485 never uses electrical signals.
options.explanation: It is an electrical interface standard.

options.text: Cable length is unaffected by the physical installation.
options.explanation: The physical layer and installation affect signal integrity.

options.text: Achievable distance depends on data rate, cable, termination, topology and the actual equipment.
options.explanation: The TI design guide explicitly relates cable length to data rate.

options.text: Every manufacturer guarantees the same distance at every rate.
options.explanation: Equipment and operating conditions can impose different limits.

questions.explanation: TI gives an approximately 1,200 m example under stated conditions and explains the distance/data-rate trade-off. Use the installed system’s limits; do not turn an approximate headline value into a guarantee.
questions.revisionNote: The approximate distance is retained as context, not a universal maximum for every access-control installation. The original RS-232 distance is also not a universal guarantee.

questions.question: What should a clearly visible CCTV notice normally tell people under the ICO transparency checklist?

options.text: Only the camera’s serial number.
options.explanation: That does not provide the required transparency information.

options.text: Nothing, if the camera is mounted high enough.
options.explanation: Visibility of the equipment does not remove transparency duties.

options.text: Every employee’s private password.
options.explanation: That would disclose sensitive information and is not a notice requirement.

options.text: That surveillance is operating, its purpose, who operates it and how to contact them.
options.explanation: People need understandable information about the processing and responsible organisation.

questions.explanation: Provide suitable signage and the wider privacy information required for the actual use. A sign is part of transparency, not proof that every data-protection obligation has been met.

questions.question: In England, for a non-hazardous business-waste transfer recorded on a waste transfer note, how long does GOV.UK say to keep a copy?

options.text: At least 2 years.
options.explanation: The cited waste-transfer-note guidance specifies two years.

options.text: No copy is needed once the waste leaves site.
options.explanation: The transfer record must be retained.

options.text: Exactly 4 years for every type of electrical waste record.
options.explanation: There is no universal rule of that kind in this guidance.

options.text: Only until the end of the working day.
options.explanation: That is shorter than the stated retention period.

questions.explanation: Classify the waste and your role correctly. Hazardous-waste consignment records and other WEEE responsibilities can have different requirements; this question is expressly about a non-hazardous transfer note in England.
questions.revisionNote: The uploaded blanket “WEEE paperwork = 4 years” is not reliable. Retention depends on record type, role and jurisdiction.

questions.question: A circuit is safely isolated, proved dead and prepared for a numerical low-resistance check. Which instrument setting is appropriate?

options.text: Current with the leads across the cable cores
options.explanation: This is not a resistance measurement and is an incorrect connection for current measurement.

options.text: Only the continuity buzzer, without reading its value
options.explanation: A buzzer is a threshold indication; it does not by itself establish the measured resistance.

options.text: A suitable ohmmeter or multimeter on the resistance range
options.explanation: This gives a numerical resistance reading in ohms.

options.text: AC voltage
options.explanation: A voltage range measures potential difference, not resistance.

questions.explanation: Use a suitable ohmmeter or resistance range for this low-resistance check. Record the numerical value and exact points; a beep alone is not a reading. Insulation-resistance testing is a different test requiring the appropriate instrument, procedure and test voltage.
questions.revisionNote: The condition and test type are explicit. This is neither permission to resistance-test an energised circuit nor a substitute for a specified insulation-resistance test.

questions.question: For the same conductor material, cross-sectional area and temperature, what happens to resistance when cable length doubles?

options.text: It halves
options.explanation: That is the opposite of the length relationship.

options.text: It stays unchanged
options.explanation: Length affects conductor resistance.

options.text: It always becomes zero
options.explanation: Adding conductor length cannot make a resistive conductor have zero resistance.

options.text: It doubles
options.explanation: R = ρL/A, so resistance is proportional to length under the stated conditions.

questions.explanation: The material, area and temperature must be comparable. A longer cable generally has greater resistance and hence more voltage drop at the same current.

questions.question: What does BAFE’s current name expand to?

options.text: British Approvals for Fire Excellence

options.explanation: This is not BAFE’s current official name.

options.explanation: This is not the organisation’s name.

options.explanation: BAFE is concerned with fire safety certification, not an electrical-fuse authority.

questions.explanation: BAFE operates the BAFE Fire Safety Register. Its current name is British Approvals for Fire Excellence.

questions.question: You are selecting readers for an access-control installation described as Grade 3. What is the defensible way to confirm the required reader/authentication technology?

options.text: Treat the intruder-alarm grade as the reader specification
options.explanation: Access control and intruder alarms have different applicable requirements.

options.text: Check the applicable access-control requirements, risk assessment and documented system design
options.explanation: The system grade and design requirements must establish the supported authentication method.

options.text: Assume every Grade 3 system must use fingerprints
options.explanation: A grade label alone does not justify that blanket claim.

options.text: Use whichever reader looks most secure
options.explanation: Appearance does not establish security performance or compliance.

questions.explanation: Confirm the actual system requirements and evidence for the chosen reader and credentials. Do not infer compliance from a manufacturer name, appearance or a remembered slogan.
questions.revisionNote: The guide states that Grade 3 access control MUST be biometric. That universal statement was not established by the current public sources; the question now tests documented selection rather than an unsupported rule.

questions.question: For Paxton Net2 logical anti-passback at an area boundary, which arrangement is required?

options.text: A permanently unlocked door
options.explanation: That defeats controlled entry rather than implementing anti-passback.

options.text: A sounder instead of an OUT reader
options.explanation: A sounder cannot identify which credential has left an area.

options.text: IN and OUT readers so the system records both directions
options.explanation: Logical anti-passback needs the credential’s entry and exit transitions.

options.text: An IN reader only, with no exit record
options.explanation: This does not establish the outbound transition required by logical anti-passback.

questions.explanation: Logical anti-passback checks the recorded sequence of entry and exit. It is different from timed anti-passback, which can operate without an OUT reader.
questions.revisionNote: The original “two readers” answer is scoped to logical anti-passback. It is not a rule for every anti-passback mode.

questions.question: Which cable feature can help reduce coupled electrical or radio-frequency interference when correctly selected and terminated?

options.text: A brighter outer sheath colour
options.explanation: Colour does not provide electromagnetic shielding.

options.text: Leaving every joint mechanically loose
options.explanation: Loose joints do not control interference and can create faults.

options.text: Removing the cable insulation
options.explanation: Insulation removal is not a noise-control method.

options.text: An appropriate conductive screen or shield
options.explanation: The screen can reduce interference when the installation follows the relevant design and grounding instructions.

questions.explanation: Screening is one part of interference control. Cable routing, signal reference, pair construction and correct termination also matter.

questions.question: Which sequence describes a typical CCTV coaxial cable from the centre outward?

options.text: Centre conductor, dielectric insulation, conductive screen, outer sheath
options.explanation: These are the basic concentric elements of coaxial cable.

options.text: Outer sheath, centre conductor, screen, dielectric
options.explanation: This places the layers in the wrong physical order.

options.text: Four identical unscreened twisted pairs
options.explanation: That describes a different cable construction.

options.text: Only a centre wire and an air gap, with no return conductor
options.explanation: Typical coax has a surrounding conductive screen/return and insulation.

questions.explanation: The centre conductor and surrounding conductive screen are separated by a dielectric. The outer sheath provides environmental/mechanical protection appropriate to the product.

questions.question: A supplier describes a cable only as “8-core alarm cable”. What additional information is needed before relying on its voltage and current ratings?

options.text: Only the number of devices already connected
options.explanation: Device count does not establish the cable’s permitted ratings.

options.text: The exact cable datasheet and installation conditions
options.explanation: Core count alone does not establish voltage, current, resistance or installation limits.

options.text: Nothing: all 8-core alarm cable has one universal rating
options.explanation: Different conductor sizes, materials and insulation produce different ratings.

options.text: Only the sheath colour
options.explanation: Colour is not a complete electrical specification.

questions.explanation: Identify the actual cable, conductor size/material and manufacturer ratings. Apply the circuit and installation requirements rather than treating “8-core” as an electrical rating.
questions.revisionNote: The uploaded notes list conflicting voltage figures alongside one cable example. They are not a universal rating for every eight-core alarm cable.

questions.question: For this particular cable, the approved support schedule specifies a maximum 300 mm spacing horizontally and 400 mm vertically. Are horizontal clips spaced 350 mm apart within that schedule?

options.text: Yes: any cable under 9 mm can be supported at any spacing
options.explanation: Diameter alone does not remove support requirements.

options.text: Only if the cable is painted red
options.explanation: Colour does not change the specified support spacing.

options.text: No: 350 mm exceeds the specified 300 mm horizontal maximum
options.explanation: Compare the actual orientation with its stated maximum.

options.text: Yes: the 400 mm vertical limit applies in every direction
options.explanation: The schedule specifies different limits for the two orientations.

questions.explanation: The numbers in this question are an explicit installation schedule, not a universal rule. Always use the cable/support system instructions and applicable design requirements.
questions.revisionNote: The guide’s 300/400 mm values need cable type, orientation and installation context. The question supplies that context instead of asserting universal clip spacing.

questions.question: What does HSE stand for in UK workplace health and safety?

options.explanation: This is not HSE’s name.

options.text: Hazardous Systems Examiner
options.explanation: This is not HSE’s name.

options.text: Home Security Establishment
options.explanation: This is unrelated to the workplace regulator.

options.text: Health and Safety Executive
options.explanation: This is the regulator’s official name.

questions.explanation: The Health and Safety Executive regulates workplace health and safety within its remit.

questions.question: Which pair of statutory notices can a health and safety inspector serve in appropriate circumstances?

options.text: Improvement and prohibition notices
options.explanation: Sections 21 and 22 of the 1974 Act provide these notice powers.

options.text: Warranty and purchase notices
options.explanation: These are not the relevant enforcement notices.

options.text: Marketing and renewal notices
options.explanation: These are commercial communications, not these statutory powers.

options.text: A fire certificate and an insurance quotation
options.explanation: Neither is an improvement or prohibition notice.

questions.question: Where suitable PPE is required for an employee’s work, what does PPE mean and who must provide it?

options.text: Protective paperwork evidence; no equipment is needed
options.explanation: Paperwork does not substitute for required protective equipment.

options.text: Personal protective equipment; the employer provides required suitable PPE free of charge
options.explanation: Required PPE is part of the employer’s health and safety duties.

options.text: Personal property equipment; the worker must always buy it
options.explanation: This misstates both the acronym and the employer’s duty.

options.text: Panel protection enclosure; the client always supplies it
options.explanation: PPE refers to protection worn or held by a person.

questions.explanation: PPE means personal protective equipment. It must be suitable for the risks and used with the required information, instruction and training; it does not replace higher-priority controls.

questions.question: Why must employers and workers follow safe working arrangements?

options.text: Only when an inspector is present
options.explanation: Duties apply during the work, not just during inspections.

options.text: Only to protect the company’s tools
options.explanation: Workers, customers and others can be affected by work activities.

options.text: To prevent harm and meet their applicable health and safety duties
options.explanation: Safe work protects people as well as meeting legal responsibilities.

options.text: Only to make the job take longer
options.explanation: Safety arrangements are intended to control risk.

questions.explanation: Health and safety duties are broader than one set of workplace regulations. Employers and employees both have responsibilities appropriate to their roles.
questions.revisionNote: The guide cites only the Workplace Regulations. The reason is broader: preventing harm and meeting applicable duties, including the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act.

questions.question: In the manual-handling reminder TILE, what do the letters represent?

options.text: Task, Individual, Load, Environment
options.explanation: These match the principal factors to assess in a manual-handling operation.

questions.question: Which set contains the four principal safety-sign colours used for the familiar prohibition/fire-equipment, warning, mandatory and safe-condition meanings?

options.text: Red, yellow, blue and green
options.explanation: These are the familiar safety colours, interpreted with the sign shape and pictogram.

options.text: Purple, pink, orange and brown
options.explanation: These are not that standard set of safety-sign colours.

options.explanation: Safety signs rely on consistent recognised meanings.

questions.question: What should an as-fitted drawing or specification describe?

options.text: A different site with similar equipment
options.explanation: Another site cannot establish this installation’s arrangement.

options.text: The system actually installed, including agreed changes
options.explanation: It records the completed installation rather than an abandoned earlier proposal.

options.text: Only the first sales sketch, even if the installation changed
options.explanation: That may no longer represent the actual system.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of electrical resistance, including a resistance reading on a detection circuit?

options.text: Ampere (A)
options.explanation: Amperes measure current.

options.text: Watt (W)
options.explanation: Watts measure power.

options.text: Ohm (Ω)
options.explanation: Resistance is expressed in ohms or suitable multiples such as kΩ.

options.text: Volt (V)
options.explanation: Volts measure potential difference.

questions.explanation: Record resistance with its unit and exact test points. A resistance value is not automatically the correct EOL value for a particular panel.

questions.question: For a fire-alarm circuit whose design requires fire-resisting cable, what should be selected?

options.text: Any red cable, regardless of its performance
options.explanation: Colour alone does not establish fire performance.

options.text: Any ordinary flexible cord because it has insulation
options.explanation: Ordinary insulation does not establish required circuit survival in fire.

options.text: A cable selected only because its diameter fits the gland
options.explanation: Mechanical fit is only one selection requirement.

options.text: An appropriate documented fire-resisting cable and support system for that circuit
options.explanation: The specification and installation must satisfy the actual system requirements.

questions.explanation: Products such as mineral-insulated cable and specified fire-resisting cable systems may be used when appropriate. Select performance and supports from the design and applicable instructions, not a brand name alone.
questions.revisionNote: The guide names MICC/FP200 examples. The correct choice depends on the circuit and required fire performance; these examples do not make every product interchangeable.

questions.question: What do the main BS 5839-1 system-category letters M, L and P refer to?

options.text: Manual systems, life protection and property protection
options.explanation: The category letters describe those principal objectives.

options.text: Maintenance, lighting and plumbing
options.explanation: These are not the fire-alarm category meanings.

options.text: Mains, low voltage and power factor
options.explanation: Those electrical terms are not these category definitions.

options.text: Manufacturer, location and price
options.explanation: Commercial labels do not define the fire-protection category.

questions.explanation: M identifies manual systems, L life-protection systems and P property-protection systems. Their subcategories and the actual design objective must be selected correctly.

questions.question: What should inform the design of a fire or security alarm system before equipment and coverage are selected?

options.text: A guess based on a different building

options.text: The applicable risk assessment, requirements and site survey
options.explanation: These establish the risks and objectives the design needs to address.

options.text: Only the colour of the panel
options.explanation: Appearance does not define the protection requirement.

options.text: Only the cheapest device available
options.explanation: Price alone does not establish a suitable design.

questions.explanation: Use the appropriate fire or security risk information and agreed requirements. One generic assessment does not automatically establish every discipline’s design.

questions.question: Which British Standard number identifies the UK Requirements for Electrical Installations, commonly called the Wiring Regulations?

options.explanation: That concerns electronic access-control application guidelines.

options.text: BS EN 62676
options.explanation: That series concerns video surveillance systems.
This is the IET/BSI Wiring Regulations standard.

questions.question: Which is a protective feature described by GS38 for suitable voltage-test probes?

options.text: A long uninsulated metal probe shaft
options.explanation: Excess exposed metal increases accidental contact and short-circuit risk.

options.text: Damaged insulation covered only by a label

questions.question: Why may a screened cable be specified for an intruder-alarm signal circuit?

options.text: To help control electromagnetic interference
options.explanation: Correctly implemented shielding can reduce unwanted coupled signals.

options.text: To make the circuit immune to every possible fault
options.explanation: A screen does not prevent all electrical or installation faults.

options.text: To remove the need for correct device wiring
options.explanation: The core connections and reference arrangements still matter.

options.text: To give every panel the same EOL resistance
options.explanation: Screening does not determine the panel’s resistance profile.

questions.question: Where should the screen of a signal cable be terminated at the panel?

questions.question: In site-work planning, what does RAMS commonly stand for?

questions.question: Which organisation provides third-party certification of security and fire-safety service providers?

options.text: USB Implementers Forum

questions.question: Which organisation maintains the BAFE Fire Safety Register for appropriately certificated fire-safety service providers?

questions.question: What is a defensible benefit of recognised independent certification for a relevant installation service?

options.explanation: Relevant instructions still apply.

options.text: It automatically proves competence in every unrelated trade
