options.explanation: Certification is not a guarantee of error-free work.

questions.explanation: Use the correct distinction: joining an organisation and achieving independent certification are not the same. Check the scheme and current scope.
questions.revisionNote: The guide equates joining a body with being reputable. This question tests the evidenced benefit of certification without making that blanket assurance.

questions.question: Which item is intended to retain saved files when it is unplugged from the computer?

options.text: Ordinary working RAM alone
options.explanation: Normal working RAM is temporary memory and needs power to retain its contents.

options.text: A monitor display
options.explanation: A display presents information; it is not the saved-file storage device.

options.text: A keyboard key switch
options.explanation: A key switch is an input component, not file storage.

options.text: A USB flash drive
options.explanation: Flash storage is non-volatile and retains stored data without continuous computer power.

questions.explanation: Examples of persistent storage include flash drives, SSDs and network storage. Keep required backups and protect sensitive information.

questions.question: Which Microsoft application is a spreadsheet tool commonly used to organise tabular data and calculate totals?

options.text: Excel
options.explanation: Excel supports worksheets, tables and formulas.

options.text: Paint
options.explanation: Paint is primarily an image-editing application.

options.text: Calculator alone
options.explanation: Calculator is not a spreadsheet system for maintaining tabular records.

options.text: A web-browser address bar
options.explanation: An address bar is not a spreadsheet application.

questions.explanation: Excel can organise and analyse tabular data. Choose a suitable approved system for the job, especially where records need access control and reliable backups.

questions.question: In computer networking, what does IP stand for?

options.text: Input Power
options.explanation: That is an electrical phrase, not the network protocol.

options.text: Internet Protocol
options.explanation: IP is the Internet Protocol used for addressing and carrying packets between networks.

options.text: Insulation Protection
options.explanation: That is not the networking expansion of IP.

options.text: Installation Programme
options.explanation: That is not the protocol name.

questions.explanation: Context matters: IP in networking means Internet Protocol. An enclosure’s IP rating refers to ingress protection, which is a different use of the letters.

questions.question: What does USB stand for?

options.text: Unswitched Signal Breaker
options.explanation: This is not the USB expansion.

options.text: Universal System Backup
options.explanation: USB is an interface technology, not itself a backup policy.

options.text: Universal Serial Bus
options.explanation: This is the name used by the USB Implementers Forum.

options.text: Unified Security Battery
options.explanation: This is not the USB expansion.

questions.explanation: Universal Serial Bus is an interface standard. A USB connection or flash drive alone does not guarantee a complete backup.

questions.question: What is ordinary computer RAM primarily used for?

options.text: Permanent storage that never needs power
options.explanation: Ordinary working RAM is volatile, unlike persistent storage.

options.text: Converting mains electricity to 24 V
options.explanation: That is a power-supply function.

options.text: Optically detecting smoke
options.explanation: That is a detector function, not RAM’s role.

options.text: Temporary working memory for data and programs currently in use
options.explanation: RAM provides fast access to the computer’s current working data.

questions.explanation: RAM means random-access memory. In an ordinary computer, it is working memory; save important files to appropriate persistent storage.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of effective communication during a job?

options.text: To exchange information so the people involved understand what is needed
options.explanation: Communication should achieve shared understanding, not just transmit words.

options.text: To speak continuously without checking understanding
options.explanation: One-way talking may leave important misunderstandings.

options.text: To use as much unexplained jargon as possible
options.explanation: Jargon can prevent the audience from understanding.

options.text: To avoid recording any agreed action
options.explanation: Important agreements and instructions often need an appropriate written record.

questions.explanation: Communication can be spoken, written, visual and supported by non-verbal cues. Select the method and language that suit the person and purpose.

questions.question: Which is a clear example of non-verbal communication during a face-to-face conversation?

options.text: A written installation report
options.explanation: That is written communication.

options.text: Facial expression and body posture
options.explanation: These communicate cues without spoken or written words.

options.text: The words in an email
options.explanation: An email uses written language; it is not the clearest example of body-language communication.

options.text: A spoken technical explanation
options.explanation: That is spoken verbal communication.

questions.explanation: Body posture, gestures and facial expressions are non-verbal cues. Avoid assuming that a single gesture has the same meaning for every person or culture.
questions.revisionNote: The guide lists emails and letters as non-verbal. This question uses the clearer distinction between written language and non-verbal body-language cues.

questions.question: A customer does not understand technical jargon in your explanation. What is the best next step?

options.text: Assume they cannot understand because of their age or background
options.explanation: Stereotypes do not establish an individual’s communication needs.

options.text: End the conversation without agreeing what happens next
options.explanation: That leaves the information gap unresolved.

options.text: Use plain language, suitable aids and check their understanding
options.explanation: Adapt the communication to the person’s actual needs.

options.text: Repeat the same jargon more loudly
options.explanation: Volume does not resolve unfamiliar terminology.

questions.explanation: Identify the actual barrier and ask what helps. Language, noise, accessibility needs and unfamiliar terms can affect communication, but do not assume needs from a person’s identity.
questions.revisionNote: The original list of age/ethnicity/position is not a reason to stereotype a person. Test the actual barrier and adapt appropriately.

questions.question: Which response best demonstrates active listening to a customer describing an intermittent fault?

options.text: Interrupt repeatedly with a diagnosis before hearing the symptoms
options.explanation: That can miss information and create a false assumption.

options.text: Ignore their account and read only the panel label
options.explanation: Their observations may contain important fault history.

options.text: Agree to everything without checking what they mean
options.explanation: Agreement alone does not show accurate understanding.

options.text: Let them finish, summarise what you understood and ask a relevant clarifying question
options.explanation: This checks the meaning and invites missing details.

questions.explanation: Active listening includes attention, clarification and summarising. Use eye contact and other cues in a way that is comfortable and accessible for the person.

questions.question: What does commercial awareness mean for an engineer working for a service company?

options.text: Understanding how work, costs, customer value and business risks affect the organisation
options.explanation: It connects technical work with sustainable and responsible business outcomes.

options.text: Only knowing the price of one detector
options.explanation: One product price is only a small part of the commercial picture.

options.text: Ignoring customer requirements to finish as fast as possible
options.explanation: That can create rework, risk and loss of trust.

options.text: Always choosing the cheapest material regardless of suitability
options.explanation: Unsuitable materials can increase risk and total cost.

questions.explanation: Consider time, resources, customer expectations, reputation and contractual responsibilities while maintaining required safety and quality.

questions.question: Which approach best describes effective time management on a service visit?

options.text: Promise an arrival time without checking travel or access
options.explanation: Unrealistic promises undermine planning and customer confidence.

options.text: Plan and prioritise tasks, allow for constraints and communicate realistic progress
options.explanation: This uses time effectively while retaining safety and quality.

options.text: Skip checks whenever the job is running late
options.explanation: Saving time does not justify omitting necessary checks.

options.text: Do every task in a random order
options.explanation: Random sequencing can create unnecessary delay and rework.

questions.explanation: Good time management organises the work and its dependencies. It is not simply doing every action faster or omitting records.

questions.question: Why can reliable customer service provide a competitive advantage?

options.text: It makes technical competence unnecessary
options.explanation: Service and competence are both required.

options.text: It permits inaccurate promises if they sound reassuring
options.explanation: Unreliable information can damage trust and create risk.

options.text: It builds trust, supports repeat business and reduces avoidable disputes
options.explanation: Customers value dependable communication and delivery.

options.text: It guarantees every customer will always renew
options.explanation: Good service helps retention but cannot guarantee every commercial outcome.

questions.explanation: Understand the customer’s needs, explain honestly and follow through on agreed actions. Good service supports both the customer and the business.

questions.question: Before work that could disturb the fabric of a building where asbestos may be present, which information is particularly important?

options.text: Only the latest alarm event log
options.explanation: That does not establish the building’s asbestos risks.

options.text: Only the paint colour on the wall
options.explanation: Appearance does not reliably identify asbestos-containing materials.

options.text: No information if the hole will be small
options.explanation: Even a small disturbance can matter; size alone does not remove the risk.

options.text: The relevant asbestos information/register and the assessment for the planned work
options.explanation: This helps identify asbestos-containing materials and necessary controls before disturbance.

questions.explanation: Check the asbestos information and suitability of the assessment for the proposed work. Do not assume an old register establishes every hidden material or authorises disturbance.

questions.question: What is the nominal resistance of two 2.2 kΩ resistors connected in parallel?

options.text: 1.1 kΩ
options.explanation: Two equal resistors in parallel give half the individual resistance.

options.text: 4.4 kΩ
options.explanation: That is their series total.

options.text: 2.2 kΩ
options.explanation: Parallel connection changes the equivalent resistance.

options.text: 0 Ω
options.explanation: Two ordinary finite resistors do not produce a zero-ohm parallel combination.

questions.explanation: For two equal resistors, Rtotal = R/2. Component tolerance and the actual measurement conditions remain separate from this nominal arithmetic.

questions.question: In an enclosure’s IP code, what does the second characteristic numeral classify?

options.text: The resistance of the protective conductor
options.explanation: That is not the IP-code meaning.

options.text: Protection against harmful ingress of water under the specified test conditions
options.explanation: The second numeral concerns water protection.

options.text: The manufacturer’s warranty length
options.explanation: Warranty duration is not encoded by that numeral.

options.text: The device’s operating voltage
options.explanation: Voltage is a separate product specification.

questions.explanation: The first numeral concerns access/solid foreign objects; the second concerns water. An IP rating does not by itself establish resistance to every chemical, corrosion condition or outdoor environment.
questions.revisionNote: The guide says “liquids”. More precisely, the second IP numeral concerns water under specified test conditions, not all liquids or all weather effects.

questions.question: Where the design identifies a high risk of electrical noise affecting a signal cable, which measure is appropriate?

options.text: Disconnect the signal reference without checking the instructions
options.explanation: Unplanned reference changes can introduce faults.

options.text: Choose a cable solely because its sheath is thicker
options.explanation: Sheath thickness alone does not establish electromagnetic performance.

options.text: Use the specified shielded/screened signal cable and follow its routing and termination instructions
options.explanation: This addresses coupled noise as part of the complete wiring arrangement.

options.text: Bundle it indiscriminately with noisy power circuits
options.explanation: That can increase interference coupling.

questions.explanation: Shielding, pair construction, separation and reference arrangements should be selected for the actual signal and interference environment.

questions.question: Which device is a type of automatic fire detector?

options.text: A passive door-position contact used only for access control
options.explanation: That detects a door state, not smoke or heat as a fire detector.

options.text: A network switch
options.explanation: It transports data; it is not a fire detector.

options.text: A USB flash drive
options.explanation: It stores data; it does not detect fire.

options.text: An optical smoke detector
options.explanation: It detects smoke using an optical sensing method.

questions.explanation: Optical smoke, heat, flame and other specialised technologies are examples of fire detection methods. Suitability depends on the risk and environment.

questions.question: Under the EN 50131 environmental-class terminology, what does Class IV describe?

options.text: Outdoor — general
options.explanation: Class IV covers outdoor equipment exposed to the general outdoor environment.

options.text: Indoor only, with well-maintained temperature
options.explanation: That corresponds to the Class I description.

options.text: Indoor — general
options.explanation: That corresponds to the Class II description.

options.text: A security grade proving resistance to every attack
options.explanation: Environmental class and security grade are separate classifications.

questions.explanation: Class IV is outdoor — general. It is not a substitute for checking the exact product’s operating limits, installation instructions and other relevant ratings.
questions.revisionNote: Highfield’s current v5.0 kit, PDF page 23, distinguishes environmental Classes I–IV separately from security Grades 1–4.

questions.question: Which part of the BS EN 60839 series provides application guidelines for electronic access-control systems?

options.text: BS 7671 alone
options.explanation: That is the Wiring Regulations, not the specific access-control application guide.
Part 11-2 is specifically the application-guidelines standard.

options.text: BS EN 60839-11-1 alone
options.explanation: Part 11-1 covers system and component requirements; the question asks for application guidelines.
That concerns relevant domestic fire detection and alarm systems.

questions.explanation: BSI lists BS EN 60839-11-2:2015 as the electronic access-control application guidelines. Part 11-1 addresses system and component requirements.
questions.revisionNote: The guide gives only “BS EN 60839”. The specific application-guideline part is 11-2; the year 2015 can still be current, so age alone does not mean withdrawal.

questions.question: A Grade 2 detector’s instructions provide a tamper output as part of its required wiring profile. What is the purpose of connecting it correctly?

options.text: To supply extra power through the alarm output
options.explanation: A tamper output is not an extra power-supply connection.

options.text: To replace all motion detection
options.explanation: Tamper and intrusion detection serve different functions.

options.text: To report interference such as opening or removing the detector, as supported by that design
options.explanation: The tamper function monitors integrity separately from normal detection.

options.text: To make every alarm activation silent
options.explanation: Tamper monitoring does not select silent alarm operation.

questions.explanation: Follow the detector and panel wiring profile so the supported tamper conditions are monitored. Do not infer the correct EOL values or terminal arrangement from the grade alone.
questions.revisionNote: The question explicitly refers to the detector’s documented tamper provision. Exact connections, resistors and supported tamper conditions are product-specific.

questions.question: In CCTV, what is H.264/AVC principally used for?

options.text: Increasing the optical zoom of a fixed lens
options.explanation: Optical zoom is a lens function, not a compression codec.

options.text: Supplying power to a camera through Ethernet
options.explanation: PoE supplies power; AVC encodes video.

options.text: Setting the alarm panel’s access code
options.explanation: A video codec does not manage panel credentials.

options.text: Compressing video so it can be transmitted or stored more efficiently
options.explanation: AVC means Advanced Video Coding; it represents video efficiently.

questions.explanation: H.264/AVC is a video compression standard. Bitrate and picture quality depend on encoder settings and the scene; compression does not automatically reduce the image resolution.
questions.revisionNote: The guide’s “Advanced Coding” is clarified as Advanced Video Coding (AVC). Compression concerns encoded data size, not necessarily image dimensions.

questions.question: Before relying on a suitable voltage indicator to prove an isolated circuit dead, what must be established?

options.text: That the indicator works correctly, using an appropriate proving method
options.explanation: A failed indicator could otherwise give a false dead indication.

options.text: That its case is a particular colour
options.explanation: Case colour does not establish correct operation.

options.text: That a non-contact voltage pen gives no alarm
options.explanation: HSE does not accept a non-contact indicator alone for proving dead.

options.text: That the circuit worked yesterday
options.explanation: Past operation says nothing about present isolation or tester condition.

questions.explanation: HSE GS38 requires a device used to prove dead to be proved before and after use. This is one prerequisite within the full safe-isolation procedure, not a replacement for it.

questions.question: A detector combining passive infrared sensing and microwave sensing is normally described as what?

options.text: An optical beam smoke detector
options.explanation: A beam smoke detector detects smoke obscuration, not this pair of intruder sensing technologies.

options.text: A dual-technology detector
options.explanation: The detector combines two different sensing technologies.

options.text: A heat-only detector
options.explanation: Heat detection does not describe PIR plus microwave movement sensing.

options.text: A magnetic contact
options.explanation: A magnetic contact responds to a magnet/reed or other magnetic sensor arrangement.

questions.explanation: PIR and microwave are different detection methods commonly combined in dual-technology intruder detectors. Confirm the exact model’s alarm logic and settings from its manual.

questions.question: What does an LSF cable description claim about its behaviour in a fire?

options.text: That it is automatically zero-halogen and identical to every LSZH cable
options.explanation: A label alone does not establish halogen content or identical test performance.

options.text: That it cannot burn under any circumstances
options.explanation: Reduced emissions do not mean a cable is non-combustible.

options.text: Reduced smoke and fume emissions compared with the relevant conventional material
options.explanation: LSF stands for low smoke and fume; the documented test performance still matters.

options.text: That it will keep a fire alarm circuit working for any duration
options.explanation: LSF is not an unlimited circuit-integrity rating.

questions.explanation: Smoke emission, halogen/acid-gas behaviour, flame propagation and circuit integrity are different characteristics. Select a cable by its documented tests and the system specification, not an LSF label alone.
questions.revisionNote: The source point is retained, but LSF is not treated as a universal certification or as interchangeable with LSZH.

questions.question: How should the replacement fuse for a piece of equipment be selected?

options.text: Always choose any fuse slightly above the measured running current
options.explanation: Running current alone does not establish the correct protective fuse.

options.text: Fit the largest fuse that fits the holder
options.explanation: Physical fit does not establish safe protection.

options.text: Increase the fuse rating whenever a fuse blows
options.explanation: A blowing fuse may indicate a fault that must be investigated.

options.text: Use the manufacturer’s specified fuse type and rating for that equipment
options.explanation: The specified rating and characteristics provide the intended protection.

questions.explanation: Fuse selection considers the protected circuit and the manufacturer’s requirements, including normal operation and starting conditions. “Always slightly higher than current” is not a sufficient selection rule.
questions.revisionNote: The guide’s blanket fuse-rating statement is replaced with the documented selection principle; nuisance blowing must not be solved by arbitrary uprating.

questions.question: What is the primary protective function of a miniature circuit breaker (MCB)?

options.text: Automatically interrupting the circuit when the specified overcurrent conditions occur
options.explanation: An MCB provides overcurrent protection within its declared ratings and characteristics.

options.text: Measuring the battery’s remaining capacity
options.explanation: An MCB is not a battery capacity tester.

options.text: Increasing a low supply voltage
options.explanation: It is not a voltage booster.

options.text: Replacing every required residual-current protective function
options.explanation: Overcurrent protection and residual-current protection are different functions.

questions.explanation: An MCB is a resettable protective switching device for overcurrent. Its breaking capacity, rating and characteristic must suit the circuit; it is not automatically an RCD.

questions.question: Why can fitting an excessively high-rated fuse to low-current equipment be dangerous?

options.text: It makes every cable cooler under overload
options.explanation: Reduced protection can increase overheating risk, not remove it.

options.text: It may fail to provide the intended protection against overheating or fault current
options.explanation: The wrong fuse can allow damaging current to persist beyond the intended protection.

options.text: It guarantees that the equipment consumes the fuse’s rated current
options.explanation: The load determines its current; the fuse rating is not a commanded consumption.

options.text: It always lowers the supply voltage to zero
options.explanation: A larger rating does not automatically remove voltage.

questions.explanation: Use the specified fuse. A rating above the permitted value may leave the cable or equipment inadequately protected; investigate the cause of repeated operation instead of uprating it.

questions.question: In a typical thermal-magnetic MCB, what causes the two trip mechanisms to operate?

options.text: A smoke sensor opens the contacts whenever dust is present
options.explanation: Smoke sensing is not the thermal-magnetic trip principle.

options.text: A timer opens the circuit at the same time each day
options.explanation: A scheduled timer is not overload or short-circuit protection.

options.text: A thermal element responds to overload and a magnetic element responds rapidly to high short-circuit current
options.explanation: The two mechanisms provide different responses to overcurrent.

options.text: Both mechanisms measure earth resistance only
options.explanation: An overcurrent trip does not measure earth-electrode resistance.

questions.explanation: Typical thermal-magnetic MCBs combine a time-dependent thermal overload response with a faster magnetic high-current response. Exact trip curves and ratings are product-specific.
questions.revisionNote: The guide mentions only an electromagnet; this question distinguishes both mechanisms in a typical thermal-magnetic device.

questions.question: Three positive resistances, 270 Ω, 470 Ω and 550 Ω, are connected in parallel. How does the equivalent resistance compare with 270 Ω?

options.text: It is exactly 270 Ω
options.explanation: The other finite parallel branches also conduct, reducing the total.

options.text: It is 1,290 Ω
options.explanation: That is the series sum, not the parallel equivalent.

options.text: It is greater than 550 Ω
options.explanation: A parallel equivalent cannot exceed all the positive branch resistances.

options.text: It is less than 270 Ω
options.explanation: For parallel positive resistors, the added conducting paths reduce the equivalent below the smallest branch.

questions.explanation: Use 1/Rtotal = 1/270 + 1/470 + 1/550. The result is approximately 130.73 Ω, which is below the smallest branch resistance.

questions.question: In Hochiki’s BS 5839-1:2025 guide, does a 25 m ceiling exceed the generally applicable maximum for a normal-sensitivity optical beam smoke detector?

options.text: No: the table lists 25 m, but all other design and manufacturer conditions must also be satisfied
options.explanation: The guide’s normal-sensitivity beam row gives a generally applicable maximum of 25 m.

options.text: Yes: every optical beam detector is limited to 7.5 m
options.explanation: The table does not apply that heat-detector limit to normal-sensitivity beams.

options.text: No: any beam detector is suitable at any height
options.explanation: The table and manufacturer requirements impose limits.

options.text: Yes: the table limits all smoke detection to 10.5 m
options.explanation: Different smoke-detection technologies have different table entries.

questions.explanation: The table lists 25 m for normal-sensitivity optical beams. Height alone does not approve an installation: detector classification, stratification, building geometry and the applicable design/manufacturer requirements still matter.
questions.revisionNote: The guide’s one-word “Yes” is scoped to the stated detector sensitivity and current manufacturer summary, rather than treated as blanket approval.

questions.question: The approved FP200 installation detail requires fire-resisting metal supports, but only nylon ties are available. What should the installer do?

options.text: Replace the cable with any flexible lead
options.explanation: An arbitrary cable change does not resolve the support requirement.

options.text: Obtain the specified suitable supports before completing that part of the installation
options.explanation: The installation must meet its approved support arrangement.

options.text: Use the nylon ties as the sole substitute and sign off the installation
options.explanation: An unapproved substitute does not establish the required support performance.

options.text: Leave the cable unsupported because its sheath is fire-resistant
options.explanation: Cable construction does not remove the need for suitable support.

questions.explanation: Follow the approved cable/support system and manufacturer instructions. Temporary availability of materials is not evidence that a substituted support arrangement achieves the required fire performance.
questions.revisionNote: The scenario explicitly states the required support detail. It does not claim that every possible use of a nylon tie is prohibited.

questions.question: A point heat detector’s sensing element is 20 mm below a flat ceiling. Does this meet the 25–150 mm position shown in Hochiki’s BS 5839-1:2025 guide?

options.text: Yes: the quoted minimum is 2.5 mm
options.explanation: The source gives 25 mm, not 2.5 mm.

options.text: No: the element must be at least 600 mm below the ceiling
options.explanation: The cited heat-detector range is 25–150 mm; the smoke-detector upper distance is different.

options.text: No: 20 mm is less than the stated 25 mm minimum
options.explanation: The position is outside the range given in the cited guide.

options.text: Yes: being closer to the ceiling always improves compliance
options.explanation: A smaller distance does not satisfy a specified minimum.

questions.explanation: The cited guide places the heat sensing element 25–150 mm below the ceiling. Check the sensing element position, not just the outer housing, and apply the actual design and manufacturer instructions.

questions.question: For a lens focused at infinity, the distance from its principal plane to the image plane is described by which optical quantity?

options.text: Working distance
options.explanation: Working distance is the distance between the lens and the subject, not the principal plane to image plane.

options.text: Cable transmission distance
options.explanation: That describes a signal link, not the lens geometry.

options.text: Frame rate
options.explanation: Frame rate is images per unit time, not a length.

options.text: Focal length
options.explanation: This is the optical definition relevant to an image formed from parallel incoming rays.

questions.explanation: Focal length is measured in millimetres and influences field of view for a given sensor size. At finite object distances, the lens-to-sensor spacing is not automatically equal to focal length.
questions.revisionNote: The original wording “when the subject is in focus” is incomplete; the infinity-focus condition avoids teaching an incorrect general definition.

questions.question: What is the upper exposure action value for daily or weekly personal noise exposure under the UK Noise at Work Regulations?

options.text: 85 dB(A)
options.explanation: HSE identifies 85 dB(A) as the upper daily/weekly exposure action value.

options.text: 80 dB(A)
options.explanation: 80 dB(A) is the lower exposure action value.

options.text: 87 dB(A)
options.explanation: 87 dB(A) is the exposure limit value, accounting for hearing protection; it is not the upper action value.
This is not the specified daily/weekly upper exposure action value.

questions.explanation: At the upper action value, employers must provide hearing protection and hearing-protection zones as required by the regulations. The value relates to daily/weekly exposure, not any single momentary sound reading.
questions.revisionNote: The question distinguishes averaged exposure, action values and the exposure limit; it does not infer fire-alarm VAD requirements from noise legislation.

questions.question: What does RFID stand for?

options.text: Recorder frame integration device
options.explanation: RFID is not a CCTV recording-rate term.

options.text: Radio-frequency identification
options.explanation: RFID uses radio-frequency communication for identification.

options.text: Remote fire indicator display
options.explanation: That is not the expansion of RFID.

options.text: Resistance fault isolation detector
options.explanation: That is not what the acronym means.

questions.explanation: RFID is radio-frequency identification. In access control, the exact credential technology and reader compatibility still need to be checked.

questions.question: A cable route into an external compound needs mechanical protection against abrasion and impact. Which cable feature is specifically intended to help provide mechanical protection?

options.text: Any thin unsheathed signal pair
options.explanation: An unprotected pair does not provide the required mechanical barrier.

options.text: A larger identification label
options.explanation: Labelling identifies a cable; it does not protect it mechanically.

options.text: Suitable steel-wire armour in a cable rated for the installation
options.explanation: Armouring can provide mechanical protection when correctly selected and installed.

options.text: A printed LSF label by itself
options.explanation: Smoke/fume performance does not establish mechanical protection.

questions.explanation: A suitable armoured cable is one possible engineered solution. Also check voltage rating, environment, bend radius, glands, earthing/bonding requirements and the actual mechanical risks.
questions.revisionNote: SWA is not an automatic answer for every duct or low-voltage circuit; the question asks which feature provides mechanical protection.

questions.question: Why may a building specification call for a cable with verified low-smoke performance?

options.text: Because low smoke means the circuit can never lose power
options.explanation: Smoke emission and circuit integrity are different properties.

options.text: Because low smoke guarantees the cable is suitable for every building
options.explanation: Suitability still depends on the specification and relevant tests.

options.text: Because it removes the need for fire detection
options.explanation: Cable emission performance does not replace detection or other fire precautions.

options.text: To reduce smoke emission during a fire compared with the specified conventional alternative
options.explanation: Lower smoke emission can support the fire strategy’s visibility and evacuation objectives.

questions.explanation: Low-smoke performance addresses smoke production. Confirm the actual test classification and any separate halogen, flame-spread and circuit-integrity requirements in the design.
questions.revisionNote: Avoid treating “LSF” as a complete specification or assuming that every PVC product has the same performance.

questions.question: For a resistive DC circuit, which formula gives current from voltage and resistance?

options.text: I = V ÷ R
options.explanation: Ohm’s law rearranges to current equals voltage divided by resistance.

options.text: I = V × R
options.explanation: Multiplying voltage by resistance does not give current.

options.text: I = R ÷ V
options.explanation: This is the reciprocal of the required relationship.

options.text: I = V + R
options.explanation: Adding quantities with different units is not Ohm’s law.

questions.explanation: With voltage in volts and resistance in ohms, I = V/R gives amperes. For example, 24 V across 120 Ω gives 0.2 A.

questions.question: What does the UK GDPR storage-limitation principle require for identifiable customer data?

options.text: Keep it until the storage device becomes full
options.explanation: Available storage is not a lawful retention criterion.

options.text: Keep it no longer than necessary for the purposes for which it is processed
options.explanation: Retention must be justified by purpose and applicable obligations.

options.text: Keep every record forever in case it might be useful
options.explanation: Indefinite retention without justification conflicts with storage limitation.

options.text: Delete every record after exactly one day
options.explanation: There is no universal one-day retention period.

questions.explanation: Set and apply a justified retention period. Legal, contractual or other valid purposes can affect it; the principle is not a universal fixed number of days.

questions.question: After completing and verifying an installation, what should form part of the handover to the customer?

options.text: Provide only an invoice, regardless of the agreed handover requirements
options.explanation: An invoice does not replace operating information and system documents.

options.text: Promise that the system will never need maintenance
options.explanation: Maintenance and future responsibilities still need to be understood.

options.text: Relevant operating information, documentation and an explanation of agreed responsibilities
options.explanation: Handover enables the customer to understand and manage the installed system.

options.text: Leave without explaining how to use the system
options.explanation: Completion of installation does not remove the need for handover.

questions.explanation: A useful handover covers the actual installed system, appropriate records and end-user operation. Required documentation varies with the system and contract.

questions.question: What best describes commercial awareness in a fire and security business?

options.text: Choosing the lowest purchase price regardless of suitability
options.explanation: Price alone ignores quality, risk and whole-job cost.

options.text: Knowing only the colour of the company vehicles
options.explanation: Brand appearance alone is not commercial awareness.

options.text: Ignoring the customer once a contract is signed
options.explanation: Customer relationships and delivery affect commercial performance.

options.text: Understanding how decisions affect customers, cost, resources, risk and business success
options.explanation: Commercial awareness connects the work to the organisation’s wider objectives.

questions.explanation: Commercial awareness includes understanding how the business provides value and remains viable. Safe, suitable and reliable delivery is part of that judgement.

questions.question: During a face-to-face explanation, which approach best supports clear communication?

options.text: Use clear language and appropriate non-verbal communication, adapted to the customer
options.explanation: Words, tone, expression and gestures can all affect understanding.

options.text: Use the same technical jargon with every customer
options.explanation: Language needs to suit the audience and context.

options.text: Assume a nod always proves complete understanding
options.explanation: A nod alone does not confirm that a complex point was understood.

options.text: Ignore the customer’s communication needs
options.explanation: Ignoring those needs can create barriers to understanding.

questions.explanation: Adapt communication to the person and confirm understanding. Non-verbal cues vary by person and culture; do not make rigid assumptions about them.
questions.revisionNote: The guide’s “always” is replaced with an inclusive, context-sensitive approach.

questions.question: Which document would normally help an end user operate a newly handed-over alarm system?

options.text: No instructions if the display lights up
options.explanation: A powered display is not a substitute for user information.

options.text: The applicable user operating manual or instructions
options.explanation: These explain the system’s permitted user operation and indications.

options.text: Only a leaflet for a different model
options.explanation: Instructions must apply to the installed equipment.

options.text: An unrelated delivery driver’s route plan
options.explanation: It does not explain use of the alarm system.

questions.explanation: Provide instructions that apply to the installed model and configuration, along with the other documents required by the system’s handover arrangements.

questions.question: A drawing updated to show the equipment and routes actually installed is usually called what?

options.text: A blank commissioning certificate
options.explanation: A certificate is not a layout drawing.

options.text: A supplier’s generic product photograph
options.explanation: A photograph of a product does not map the installed system.

options.text: An as-fitted or as-built drawing
options.explanation: It records the installation as it exists after the work.

options.text: An unamended tender sketch
options.explanation: An early sketch may not show the final installation.

questions.explanation: As-fitted records support operation, future maintenance and subsequent work. Changes from the original design should be properly recorded and authorised.

questions.question: What is an important purpose of a system logbook?

options.text: To replace every manufacturer manual
options.explanation: A logbook records the system history; it does not contain all product instructions.

options.text: To conceal unresolved faults from the next engineer
options.explanation: Unresolved matters should be recorded clearly.

options.text: To record only the installer’s lunch breaks
options.explanation: That does not provide the relevant system history.

options.text: To maintain a dated history of tests, events, faults, maintenance and relevant actions
options.explanation: The history helps users and engineers understand what happened and what remains outstanding.

questions.explanation: Entries should be clear enough for another competent person to follow the system’s history. A cleared indication alone does not document the cause or repair.

questions.question: What serious consequence can follow an offence such as unlawfully depositing controlled waste?

options.text: Prosecution, with penalties that can include a fine or imprisonment
options.explanation: Environmental Protection Act offences can carry criminal penalties.

options.text: An automatic exemption because the offender was busy
options.explanation: Being busy does not create a legal exemption.

options.text: Only a requirement to change uniform
options.explanation: Environmental offences are not limited to an internal clothing issue.

options.text: Guaranteed immunity if the waste came from an alarm installation
options.explanation: The origin of the work does not remove environmental duties.

questions.explanation: The exact offence, jurisdiction and court determine the penalty. Proper waste handling protects people and the environment as well as the business.

questions.question: Which response best demonstrates active listening when a customer describes a fault?

options.text: Change the subject whenever the customer mentions a concern
options.explanation: Avoiding the concern prevents useful communication.

options.text: Let them explain, then summarise the concern and ask focused clarifying questions
options.explanation: This checks understanding without assuming the answer.

options.text: Interrupt immediately with a diagnosis before hearing the symptoms
options.explanation: That can miss relevant information and discourage the customer.

options.text: Promise that there cannot be a fault because the panel is powered
options.explanation: Power alone does not establish that the whole system is healthy.

questions.explanation: Active listening means attending to the person, checking what they mean and responding appropriately. Eye contact can be helpful for some people but is not a universal requirement.
questions.revisionNote: The explanation avoids making direct eye contact a requirement for every person or situation.

questions.question: What is the equivalent resistance of two 2 kΩ resistors connected in parallel?

options.text: 2 kΩ
options.explanation: Both parallel branches conduct, so the equivalent is below either one.

options.text: 0 Ω
options.explanation: Finite positive resistors in parallel do not create a zero-ohm short.

options.text: 1 kΩ
options.explanation: Two equal resistances in parallel give half the value of either resistor.

options.text: 4 kΩ
options.explanation: 4 kΩ is their series sum.

questions.question: Under section 2 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act, what general duty does an employer owe employees?

options.text: Guarantee that no employee can ever suffer any illness anywhere
options.explanation: The duty concerns work and is qualified by reasonably practicable measures.

options.text: Protect only employees who ask in writing
options.explanation: The general duty does not depend on a written request.

options.text: Transfer all safety responsibility to the newest apprentice
options.explanation: Delegating tasks does not remove the employer’s duty.

options.text: Ensure, so far as reasonably practicable, their health, safety and welfare at work
options.explanation: This is the general statutory duty stated in section 2.

questions.explanation: The duty includes matters such as safe systems, information, instruction, training and supervision. Employees also have their own responsibilities.

questions.question: What does regulation 4 of the Electricity at Work Regulations require concerning the maintenance of electrical systems?

options.text: Maintenance, so far as reasonably practicable, as may be necessary to prevent danger
options.explanation: The regulation links maintenance to preventing danger.

options.text: Maintenance only after an electric shock has occurred
options.explanation: The duty is preventive, not limited to action after harm.

options.text: No maintenance if the system was new when installed
options.explanation: New equipment can deteriorate or be affected by its use and environment.

options.text: A fixed identical inspection interval for every electrical system
options.explanation: The regulation does not prescribe one universal interval for all systems.

questions.explanation: The required maintenance depends on the system, its use and the risk. It should prevent danger rather than merely keep equipment operating.

questions.question: In England, a workplace with 10 or more full-time-equivalent employees is arranging waste collections in November 2026. Which approach matches Simpler Recycling requirements?

options.text: Ignore the rules until March 2027 because every business has that deadline
options.explanation: The later deadline is for micro-firms with fewer than 10 full-time-equivalent employees.

options.text: Separate the required food waste, dry recyclable waste and residual waste streams using the applicable collection arrangements
options.explanation: The current England workplace rules require separation of these waste streams.

options.text: Put all food, recyclables and residual waste together by default
options.explanation: That does not meet the required separation arrangements.

options.text: Assume only households have recycling requirements
options.explanation: The cited rules apply to workplaces as well.

questions.explanation: England’s workplace separation requirements generally applied from 31 March 2025; micro-firms have until 31 March 2027. Paper/card normally require a separate collection from other dry recyclables unless the applicable assessment allows joint collection. Other UK nations have their own rules.
questions.revisionNote: The older guide’s single 2020 legislation reference is not a complete statement of current requirements. The question now states jurisdiction, workforce size and date.

questions.question: Which cable characteristic can help reduce electromagnetic interference affecting a signal circuit when correctly installed?

options.text: Leaving every screen disconnected regardless of the equipment manual
options.explanation: An arbitrary termination rule may defeat the designed screening arrangement.

options.text: Increasing the printed font size on the cable
options.explanation: Printed markings do not provide electromagnetic shielding.

options.text: Suitable screening or shielding with the specified termination arrangement
options.explanation: A screen can reduce unwanted coupling when the cable and bonding arrangement suit the system.

options.text: Choosing a cable only because its jacket is bright yellow
options.explanation: Jacket colour alone does not establish electromagnetic performance.

questions.explanation: Use the cable and screen termination specified for the equipment and environment. Screening does not remove the need for appropriate segregation, routing and installation.

questions.question: A remote fire-panel unit is designed to issue authorised silence and reset commands to the main system. What description best fits it?

options.text: An indication-only passive display with no controls
options.explanation: An indication-only unit cannot provide the stated control commands.

options.text: A detector end-of-line resistor
options.explanation: An EOL component supervises a circuit; it is not a remote control panel.

options.text: A battery charger only
options.explanation: A charger does not provide those system control functions.

options.text: An active repeater or remote control-and-indicating unit
options.explanation: Its control functions distinguish it from indication-only equipment.

questions.explanation: An active repeater can provide the control functions documented for that particular system and access level. Confirm what the installed unit actually supports.

questions.question: Why should engineers follow applicable industry and company codes of practice?

options.text: To support consistent, competent work and fulfil the applicable requirements
options.explanation: Following relevant procedures supports quality, accountability and confidence.

options.text: To avoid reading the equipment’s own instructions
options.explanation: Applicable company procedures do not remove product-specific requirements.

options.text: To guarantee that no inspection will ever be needed
options.explanation: Compliance and quality still need checking.

options.text: To make every installation identical regardless of risk or design
options.explanation: Different installations can require different designs and measures.

questions.explanation: Use the applicable codes, approved design and manufacturer instructions together. Where requirements conflict or are unclear, resolve the issue rather than choosing arbitrarily.

questions.question: Which type of device can give a technician mobile access to authorised job records, messages and work progress?

options.text: An unpowered magnetic contact
options.explanation: It does not manage job records or messages.

options.text: A suitable configured smartphone, tablet or handheld work terminal
options.explanation: Modern mobile work devices can support those applications.

options.text: A passive end-of-line resistor
options.explanation: It has no user interface or job-management application.

options.text: A standalone thermal fuse
options.explanation: It is a protective component, not a communications device.

questions.explanation: The older guide uses “PDA”. A current equivalent is an appropriately secured mobile work device with authorised applications and access.
questions.revisionNote: Terminology is updated from PDA without changing the underlying electronic job-management point.

questions.question: Three 2.2 Ω resistors are connected in series. What is their total resistance?

options.explanation: Each series resistor contributes to the total.
The sum does not produce a tenfold increase.
Series resistances add: 2.2 + 2.2 + 2.2.
That is approximately the equivalent of three equal 2.2 Ω resistors in parallel.

questions.explanation: For series resistors, Rtotal = R1 + R2 + R3 = 6.6 Ω. Keep Ω and kΩ distinct.

questions.question: After installation, which stage normally includes configuring the system and testing that it functions as designed?

options.text: Only the initial sales enquiry
options.explanation: The installed system does not yet exist at that stage.

options.text: Only disposal at the end of its life
options.explanation: Commissioning occurs before normal handover/use, not only at disposal.

options.text: The invoice payment stage alone
options.explanation: Payment does not establish correct functional operation.

options.text: Commissioning
options.explanation: Commissioning verifies the installed system against the design and requirements.

questions.explanation: Competent commissioning includes the relevant configuration, functional tests and records. It is more than simply switching the power on.

questions.question: Which source most directly states the storage-limitation principle used to decide retention of identifiable personal data?

options.text: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(e), considered with applicable data-protection law and obligations
options.explanation: The storage-limitation principle is expressly set out in Article 5.

options.text: A camera’s image resolution setting
options.explanation: Image resolution does not establish a lawful retention period.

options.text: The capacity printed on the hard drive
options.explanation: Storage capacity is not a legal retention rule.

options.text: A rule that every record must be kept for the owner’s lifetime
options.explanation: There is no such universal retention rule.

questions.explanation: The Data Protection Act 2018 forms part of the wider UK framework, but retention should be justified by the data’s purpose and relevant obligations, using the storage-limitation principle.
questions.revisionNote: The source guide names the Data Protection Act 2018; this question points directly to the relevant UK GDPR principle and avoids implying one fixed statutory retention period.

questions.question: What is a likely commercial benefit of building strong, positive customer relationships?

options.text: A guarantee that every customer will buy every future offer
options.explanation: Repeat business is an opportunity, not a certainty.

options.text: Greater trust, a stronger reputation and opportunities for repeat business
options.explanation: Positive relationships can support customer retention and recommendations.

options.text: A guarantee that maintenance will never be needed
options.explanation: Good relationships do not change equipment maintenance needs.

options.text: Permission to ignore agreed work requirements
options.explanation: Trust does not remove contractual or technical responsibilities.

questions.explanation: Reliable service and clear communication help maintain trust. Their commercial benefits are likely outcomes, not guarantees.

questions.question: What business risk can arise from an installation-company representative behaving inappropriately towards a customer?

options.text: Removal of all legal and contractual obligations
options.explanation: Poor conduct does not remove those obligations.

options.text: Guaranteed reduction in all operating costs
options.explanation: There is no such guaranteed saving and costs may increase.

options.text: Reputational damage and loss of existing or future business
options.explanation: A representative’s conduct can affect trust in the whole organisation.

options.text: Automatic improvement in customer confidence
options.explanation: Inappropriate conduct usually undermines confidence.

questions.explanation: Professional behaviour is part of service quality and commercial risk management. Follow the organisation’s conduct and complaint procedures.

questions.question: What is a main purpose of good communication within an installation team?

options.text: Guarantee that no disagreement can ever occur
options.explanation: People can still disagree; good communication helps resolve it.

options.text: Remove the need to report changes
options.explanation: Changes need to be communicated and recorded appropriately.

options.text: Ensure only one person ever knows the work plan
options.explanation: Withholding relevant information obstructs coordination.

options.text: Make roles, work requirements, changes and concerns clear so the team can coordinate
options.explanation: Shared understanding supports coordinated and safer work.

questions.explanation: Good team communication helps people understand their responsibilities and raise concerns. It reduces misunderstandings but cannot guarantee complete agreement.
questions.revisionNote: The guide’s claim that communication ensures no disagreements is not used as an absolute answer.

questions.question: What is the principal role of network-attached storage (NAS)?

options.text: Provide file storage that authorised devices can access over a network
options.explanation: NAS makes stored files available through network services.

options.text: Supply PoE power to every camera
options.explanation: NAS is storage, not automatically a PoE power source.

options.text: Replace every network switch
options.explanation: Storage and Ethernet switching are different functions.

options.text: Guarantee a backup simply because files are on it
options.explanation: A NAS is not automatically an independent backup strategy.

questions.explanation: NAS is network-attached file storage. Permissions, resilience and backups must be configured; being network-connected does not itself protect against all data loss.

questions.question: Which transport protocol uses sequence numbers, acknowledgements and retransmission to provide a reliable, ordered byte stream?

options.text: An optical zoom setting
options.explanation: A lens setting is not a network transport protocol.

options.text: TCP
options.explanation: TCP uses these mechanisms to detect and recover from loss within a connection.

options.text: UDP by itself
options.explanation: UDP does not itself provide TCP’s ordered, retransmitted byte-stream service.

options.text: IP addressing alone
options.explanation: IP addressing and routing do not provide TCP’s transport reliability mechanisms.

questions.explanation: TCP provides reliability mechanisms and reports connection failure when recovery cannot succeed. It does not guarantee that every attempted transfer will succeed on a failed network.
questions.revisionNote: The original “TCP/IP so no data is lost” is narrowed to TCP’s actual role; it is not an absolute delivery guarantee.

questions.question: After preventive or corrective maintenance, where should the relevant system history and outstanding matters be recorded?

options.text: Only on an unrelated supplier’s advertisement
options.explanation: That is not a system maintenance record.

options.text: Nowhere if the fault indication has cleared
options.explanation: A cleared indication does not remove the need to record work and uncertainty.

options.text: In the appropriate system logbook and maintenance/service records
options.explanation: These records let the user and the next engineer see the work and remaining issues.

options.text: Only in the engineer’s memory
options.explanation: Memory is not a durable shared record.

questions.explanation: Record the work, tests, results and any impairments or outstanding actions accurately. Use the required logbook/service record arrangements for the system.

questions.question: Which item would normally NOT form part of the client’s technical alarm-system handover pack?

options.text: The required as-fitted drawings and device-location information
options.explanation: These can be required to understand and maintain the installed system.

options.text: The applicable user operating instructions
options.explanation: The user needs relevant instructions for the system.

options.text: The relevant commissioning and handover records
options.explanation: These document what was checked and handed over.

options.text: The contractor’s private staff payroll records
options.explanation: Payroll information is not part of the installed system’s technical handover.

questions.explanation: Required technical documents can include operating instructions, as-fitted/device information and commissioning records. The current Highfield kit explicitly includes a circuit list and marked drawing; applicable fire handover guidance also addresses cause-and-effect information.
questions.revisionNote: The older guide suggests that device lists and as-fitted drawings are least likely to be provided. That conflicts with the cited handover guidance, so the corrected question preserves the documentation topic without teaching that exclusion.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of commissioning an installed alarm system?

options.text: Demonstrate and record that it operates as designed and meets the applicable requirements
options.explanation: Commissioning uses relevant checks and functional tests to establish the installed operation.

options.text: Prove only that the power LED illuminates
options.explanation: Power indication alone does not verify system functions.

options.text: Avoid testing interfaces because they were bought new
options.explanation: New interfaces still need the required verification.

options.text: Guarantee that a fault can never occur in future
options.explanation: Commissioning is not a guarantee against future faults or deterioration.

questions.explanation: Commissioning should be performed by competent people against the approved design and applicable procedures, with results and unresolved issues recorded.

questions.question: Before starting a work task, what is the most appropriate way to protect yourself and others?

options.text: Continue with an unfamiliar hazardous task without seeking guidance
options.explanation: Lack of competence or information must be resolved before proceeding.

options.text: Understand the hazards and apply the required controls, competence and safe-working arrangements
options.explanation: Risk assessment and safe methods address the actual task and environment.

options.text: Rely on luck if the task should only take a minute
options.explanation: A short task can still involve serious hazards.

options.text: Assume PPE makes every task safe regardless of other controls
options.explanation: PPE does not replace eliminating or controlling risks where required.

questions.explanation: Work within your competence and the agreed safe system. If conditions or hazards are different from those assessed, stop and reassess rather than improvising.

questions.question: What is the usual positioning rule for a leaning ladder against a suitable surface?

options.text: Place it vertically without securing it
options.explanation: A vertical unsecured leaning ladder does not follow the rule.

options.text: Any angle is acceptable if a second person is nearby
options.explanation: A second person does not make an unsuitable angle acceptable.

options.text: One unit out for every four units up, approximately 75°
options.explanation: HSE gives the 1-in-4 rule for the correct angle.

options.text: One unit out for every one unit up, approximately 45°
options.explanation: That is much shallower than the recommended leaning-ladder angle.

questions.explanation: HSE’s 1-in-4 rule gives approximately 75°. Ladder suitability, condition, footing, securing and the task still need to be checked.

questions.question: What should identifying hazards and applying effective risk controls achieve?

options.text: Guarantee zero risk in every circumstance
options.explanation: A risk assessment is not a universal zero-risk guarantee.

options.text: Make unsafe equipment acceptable without repair
options.explanation: Paperwork cannot repair or make defective equipment safe.

options.text: Remove the need to review changes in the task
options.explanation: Changed conditions may require reassessment and revised controls.

options.text: Reduce the likelihood and/or severity of harm, with controls reviewed as needed
options.explanation: Risk controls are intended to prevent or reduce harm.

questions.explanation: Risk assessment is part of managing risk: identify hazards, assess who may be harmed and how, control risks, record findings where required, and review the controls.

questions.question: A contractor agrees an important change with a subcontractor. What best reduces later misunderstanding?

options.text: Record the agreed change clearly and confirm that both parties understand it.
options.explanation: A clear written record preserves what was agreed; confirmation checks understanding.

options.text: Rely only on an informal conversation.
options.explanation: A conversation alone leaves no dependable record of the change.

options.text: Send an unexplained drawing and assume it has been understood.
options.explanation: Sending information does not establish shared understanding.

options.text: Wait until the final invoice to mention it.
options.explanation: The team needs the agreed requirements before doing the work.

questions.explanation: Use clear, appropriate communication and record important requirements or changes. Written information supports, rather than replaces, checking understanding.
questions.revisionNote: The revision guide says information should always be written. The question focuses on recording an important agreed change; verbal communication can still be appropriate.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the final handover of an alarm system?

options.text: Leave the system in an engineering test mode.
options.explanation: Temporary conditions must be resolved or explicitly managed and recorded.

options.text: Give the responsible users the information, demonstrations and records needed to operate and manage it.
options.explanation: Handover transfers usable knowledge and the required documentation to the customer.

options.text: Demonstrate every installer programming option to every user.
options.explanation: Users need appropriate operating instruction; unrestricted engineering access is not the purpose.

options.text: Collect payment without discussing operation.
options.explanation: Commercial completion does not replace the technical handover.

questions.explanation: Handover should explain normal operation, responses to signals, limitations, responsibilities and the relevant records. It is not simply handing over keys.

questions.question: Which three letters identify the main BS 5839-1 fire-alarm category groups?

options.text: I, II and III.
options.explanation: Roman numerals may identify other classifications, not these groups.

options.text: F, S and E.
options.explanation: These letters do not identify the main BS 5839-1 categories.

options.text: M, L and P.
options.explanation: M is manual, L primarily protects life, and P primarily protects property.

options.text: A, B and C.
options.explanation: These are not the three BS 5839-1 category groups.

questions.explanation: The main groups are M, L and P; L and P have subcategories with different coverage objectives.

questions.question: A residential care building has sleeping accommodation for 12 people who need staff assistance to evacuate. Which system type does the cited 2025 guide recommend?

options.text: A non-addressable system solely because it is cheaper.
options.explanation: Cost alone does not satisfy the stated care-premises recommendation.

options.text: Only standalone domestic smoke alarms.
options.explanation: That is not the system described for this scenario.

options.text: No detection if staff are always present.
options.explanation: Staff presence does not remove the need for the specified protection.

options.text: An addressable fire detection and alarm system.
options.explanation: The guide recommends addressable detection for this assisted-evacuation situation above ten sleeping occupants.

questions.explanation: The example deliberately uses 12 sleeping occupants so it is clearly above the threshold in the guide. Address information helps staff locate the origin of an alarm.
questions.revisionNote: The uploaded question uses ten or more. The cited manufacturer guide has inconsistent wording at the exact boundary, so this question uses an unambiguous above-ten scenario; confirm the actual design against the standard.

questions.question: Which action is normally part of the weekly user test of a manual-call-point fire alarm system, after the required notifications and arrangements?

options.text: Operate an appropriate manual call point and check the system response under the documented test procedure.
options.explanation: This exercises the system from an initiating device rather than just a panel indicator.

options.text: Only press the panel lamp-test button.
options.explanation: A lamp test does not demonstrate the response to a call point.

options.text: Disconnect all standby batteries each week.
options.explanation: That is not the normal weekly user test described.

options.text: Trigger a detector with an uncontrolled flame.
options.explanation: That is unsafe and is not an approved test method.

questions.explanation: Follow the system instructions, notify any alarm receiving centre as required, use the test arrangements and restore the system afterwards. Record the test in the logbook.

questions.question: Who publishes the British Standard BS 5839 code-of-practice series?

options.text: The customer’s insurer alone.
options.explanation: Insurer requirements can supplement a design brief but do not make the insurer the standards publisher.

options.text: BSI, the British Standards Institution.
options.explanation: BSI publishes British Standards, including this series.

options.text: The local alarm receiving centre.
options.explanation: An ARC receives signals; it does not publish British Standards.

options.text: The individual panel manufacturer.
options.explanation: Manufacturers publish product instructions and guides, not the British Standard itself.

questions.explanation: BS 5839-1 concerns non-domestic premises. Other parts have other scopes, so state the applicable part and edition.

questions.question: For an initial sounder assessment, what approximate attenuation through a closed fire door is quoted in the cited fire-alarm guide?

options.text: No attenuation because a fire door is certified.
options.explanation: A fire rating does not mean sound passes through unchanged.

options.text: A guaranteed increase of 30 dB(A).
options.explanation: The quoted effect is a reduction, not amplification.

options.text: Approximately 30 dB(A), with the actual installation still requiring verification.
options.explanation: The guide quotes approximately 30 dB(A) as an expectation, not a guaranteed measurement.

options.text: Exactly 30 dB(A) for every fire door.
options.explanation: Actual attenuation depends on the door and installation; the guide says approximately.

questions.explanation: Do not use an approximate door allowance as proof of adequate audibility at the required locations. Verify the system under the relevant closed-door conditions.
questions.revisionNote: The uploaded answer is a useful approximate planning figure, not a universal measured loss for every fire door.

questions.question: What is the normal target interval for periodic inspection and servicing described in the FIA guide to BS 5839-1:2025?

options.text: Exactly once every two years.
options.explanation: That is not the periodic interval described in the cited guide.

options.text: Only after a fault appears.
options.explanation: Corrective call-outs do not replace periodic inspection and servicing.

options.text: Any interval is acceptable if the weekly test passes.
options.explanation: User testing does not remove the servicing requirement.

options.text: Approximately six months, with the stated five-to-seven-month scheduling allowance.
options.explanation: The current guide explains the six-month target and the permitted scheduling window.

questions.explanation: A six-month programme normally means two scheduled visits per year. The 2025 guidance gives a five-to-seven-month allowance anchored to the acceptance datum; the maintenance plan and relevant requirements still apply.
questions.revisionNote: Updated from the guide’s shorthand “two visits / every six months” to include the 2025 scheduling clarification. This does not mean every test is simply divided into two identical halves.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a fire-alarm zone plan?

options.text: Help responders quickly locate the area indicated by the alarm.
options.explanation: A correctly orientated plan connects the panel’s zone indication to the physical building.

options.text: Show the engineer’s private access code.
options.explanation: A zone plan is not a place to publish access credentials.

options.text: Replace the fire risk assessment.
options.explanation: A location plan does not perform a risk assessment.

options.text: Prove that every detector is currently healthy.
options.explanation: A plan shows locations; it does not establish live device condition.

questions.explanation: The plan should make the relevant zones and locations understandable without unnecessary searching. Keep it accurate when the building or system changes.

questions.question: Is “24 hours” by itself enough to specify the correct standby battery for every fire-alarm installation?

options.text: No; all systems always require 72 hours instead.
options.explanation: Replacing one blanket assumption with another is not a valid design method.

options.text: No. Use the applicable standby and alarm durations, measured or documented loads, allowances and equipment limits.
options.explanation: Duration alone does not establish the ampere-hour capacity or the correct design requirement.

options.text: Yes; every panel uses the same battery capacity.
options.explanation: Different loads, operating periods and charger limits produce different requirements.

options.text: Yes; only the battery voltage matters.
options.explanation: Voltage and available capacity are different quantities.

questions.explanation: The source manual calculates standby from quiescent and alarm loads and capacity. Confirm the applicable design category, monitoring arrangements, durations and charger/battery constraints before selecting a battery.
questions.revisionNote: The uploaded answer gives 24 hours in a particular context. It must not become an unconditional rule for every system or a substitute for the full battery calculation.

questions.question: What normal manual-call-point mounting position is stated in the cited BS 5839-1:2025 pocket guide?

options.text: Always 2.5 m above the floor.
